text: Amelia County Board of Supervisors Retreat — September 18, 2026 AMELIA COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS RETREAT Friday, September 18, 2026 SEED Innovation Hub 116 South Street Farmville, Virginia 23901 AGENDA 8:30-8:45 a.m. Gather 9:00 a.m. Call to Order Introductory Remarks and Review of the Day’s Agenda SUGGESTED GOALS FOR THE RETREAT • Work as a team and develop consensus • Encourage input from all Board members • Identify major goals for the Board to pursue • Identify objectives and priorities, with assigned responsibility and timelines • Craft a work plan for the next 12 to 24 months • Identify longer-term issues • Understand constraints to progress and identify means to overcome them THEMES THAT MAY RUN THROUGH THE DAY • Board roles and responsibilities; dynamics and governance processes • Board/Administrator roles and relationships • Longer-term strategic planning for the future of Amelia County • Limitations — staff, finances, time, statutes, Dillon Rule GROUND RULES • Everyone participates; no one dominates • Engage • Be honest • Listen to each other • Respect different opinions • No idea is too outlandish • Seek to understand Page 1 of 3 Amelia County Board of Supervisors Retreat — September 18, 2026 • Ask questions • Seek consensus (formal action at a future Board meeting) • Silence means consent — speak up if you disagree • Use the “parking lot” for issues that may evade consensus or require more background • We will take breaks when it seems appropriate • Enjoy your time together, and have fun! Getting to Know Your Team • What was your motivation to serve Amelia County in your role? • If you could change one thing in Amelia County, what would it be? • What one accomplishment have you seen during your time on the Board that you are particularly proud of? • What do you like to do for fun? Roles and Responsibilities – Board Members and County Administrator Discussion of County Vision (from the Comprehensive Plan) “Protect the rural character, cultural heritage, and scenic beauty of the County. Recognize that these are valuable and irreplaceable resources.” Discussion of Values and Operating Principles • What is important to you in how the County operates, in citizen, Board, and staff interactions and relationships? Discussion of County Operations • What is the County doing that you are proud of? • What is the County doing that you feel needs to change? • What is it that the County is not doing that it should consider? • What is it that the County is doing that it should stop? Review of Action Items and Outcomes from 2025 Board Retreat 12:00 p.m. Break for Lunch Page 2 of 3 Amelia County Board of Supervisors Retreat — September 18, 2026 12:30 p.m. Reconvene Observations from the County Administrator Discussion of Common Themes That Emerged in Conversations with Board Members Identification of Major Goal Areas Identification of Objectives, Priorities, Timelines, and Responsible Party(ies) Under Each Goal Area • Immediate or ongoing actions • Over the next 12–24 months • Longer term (as much as 3–5 years) Steps to Ensure Success • What is needed to achieve your goals? • What assets do you have presently that can be utilized? • What limitations are you facing, if any? (staff, finances, time, consensus, commitment, statute, policy, practice, etc.) • What can you do to address the limitations? • What information would be useful to the Board to provide accountability: periodic reports, financial reports, project progress reports? • How will your plan and progress with implementation be communicated? • How, and how often, will the plan be reviewed and modified? 3:30 p.m. Wrap-Up • Is there any unfinished work? • What next steps do you want to take? Facilitator Responsibilities and Comments Final Comments from the Chair, Board Members, and the County Administrator 4:00 p.m. Adjourn Page 3 of 3

PARTICIPANTS: DAVID M. FELTS DEXTER JONES BENJAMIN MORRIS H. JOSEPH EASTER, IV TODD ROBINSON District 1 District 2 District 3 District 4 (Via Zoom) District 5 Board of Supervisors ALSO ATTENDING: ERIC S. POLLITT, COUNTY ADMINISTRATOR ASHLEY PILLAR, DEPUTY COUNTY ADMINISTRATOR / FINANCE DIRECTOR (Via Zoom) JEFF GORE, COUNTY ATTORNEY Chairman Felts called the August 26, 2026, Regular Meeting of the Amelia County Board of Supervisors to order at 7:00 P.M. and determined there was a quorum with all five members participating. Supervisor Morris offered the invocation, and everyone participated in the Pledge of Allegiance. APPROVE/AMEND THE AGENDA  Supervisor Robinson made a motion to allow Supervisor Easter to participate in the meeting by Zoom. Motion was approved unanimously.  Chairman Felts made a request to pull the 9/11 Memorial Event from the Consent Agenda and include it under Staff Reports for discussion by the Board. Supervisor Easter made a request to remove the Library Board Nominations as it did not follow Board procedures and Chairman Felts stated that it would be moved under Staff Reports for Board discussion.  Supervisor Morris made a motion to amend the consent agenda with modifications as stated by Chairman Felts previously. Motion was approved unanimously. CONSENT AGENDA o Supervisor Morris made a motion to approve the consent agenda as amended. Motion was approved unanimously. A. Approval of Minutes • July 22, 2026 Regular Meeting Minutes • July 30, 2026 Special Meeting Minutes B. Resolution of Support for Virginia Tobacco Commission- Southside Grant Program-EDA C. Amelia County Sheriff’s Office -VACORP Funds Claim #4457 RECOGNITIONS A. Post Season Baseball & Softball Teams A. Dixie Youth Baseball & Belles Softball players provided a season recap to the Board. Brian 1 Wagner spoke on behalf of Dixie Youth Baseball’s 6U and 8U teams. Jessica Brown spoke on behalf of the Belles Softball team, young ladies ages 12 through 15 years old. B. Introduction of Deputy Parks & Recreation Director- Isaiah LeBlanc A. Glen Wilkerson introduced Isaiah LeBlanc as the new Deputy Parks & Recreation Director, highlighting his experience in the field and the great addition he has been to the department to date. The Board welcomed Mr. LeBlanc. PUBLIC COMMENTS • Martin Konkel residing at 16211 Church Street, expressed interest in being involved on committees within the county. STAFF/COMMITTEE/ORGANIZATIONAL REPORTS AND PRESENTATIONS A. VDOT Report: o Adam Brooks with VDOT discussed items they are working on throughout the county. B. School Board Report: o Superintendent, Dr. Lori Harper, reported on new teachers and staff returning, the first week of school, and the future of the Amelia – Nottoway Technical Center. Enrollment is at 1,429. o Financial Reports: o Director of Finance & School Nutrition, Daniel Trump, presented financial reports as of July 31st FY26. No questions were asked. o Appropriations: o None requested. C. J.L. Hamner Library Report: o Director, Keith McFarlane provided an update for the library programming. D. Amelia Live Concert Series Report: o Deputy Director, Isaiah LeBlanc provided a report regarding event details. E. Meals Tax Implementation Update: o Finance Director, Ashley Pillar, discussed the implementation of the meals tax and provided an overview of the process and next steps. F. 2026 Annual Planning Session Retreat Update: o Craig Meadows with the Berkley Group provided details on preparation for the Board’s retreat in September. G. Special Event Permit – 9/11 Memorial: o Interim Fire Chief, Tommy Hicks presented event details, a draft agenda, and a draft proclamation to the Board for discussion. o Supervisor Easter made a motion to approve the proclamation as presented. Motion was approved unanimously. H. Committee Appointments: o Supervisor Easter stated that the process is to receive nominations two weeks in advance and contact information is provided. Those provisions were not met prior to this meeting. Chairman Felts acknowledged that the process was not followed and that it would be postponed to next month’s meeting to obtain the information. 2 FINANCE A. Action Required Appropriations a. Circuit Court Clerk’s Office- Appropriation for Temporary Staffing During Retirement Transition | Action i. Marilyn Wilson, Clerk of the Circuit Court, presented the details of the appropriation to the Board. Supervisor Morris made the motion to approve the appropriation as submitted. Chairman Felts and Supervisors Jones, Morris and Robinson approved the motion. Supervisor Easter opposed the motion. B. Informational Appropriations a. Treasurer’s Office- Budget Transfer b. J.L. Hanmer Library- Budget Transfer i. Director, Keith McFarlane provided a brief description of what the budget transfer was for and how it would enable library staff to serve patrons more efficiently while saving time. COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT A. Community Development Monthly Report B. Environmental Department Report C. DMV Agent Compensation Statement and Payment Report COUNTY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT A. COAD Monthly Report a. County Administrator Eric Politt provided a monthly report. He discussed some follow up administrative items he is working on with the County Attorney Jeff Gore for the September’s meeting and working with Craig Meadows on the upcoming Board Retreat scheduled for September 18th. B. YTD FY26 Waste Management Host Fees a. Monthly fees are $218,737.02. OLD BUSINESS A. Solid Waste Ordinance | Action o Supervisor Morris made the motion to direct staff to proceed with issuing the public notice to amend Part 1, Chapter 164, Article V, §164-34, letter H of the Amelia County Code of Ordinances. Motion was approved unanimously. NEW BUSINESS A. Public Hearing - Special Exception Permit- SEP26-01 | Action o Darla Odom with the Berkley Group presented the details of the request to the Board. o Chairman Felts opened the Public Hearing. The current landowner, Kathleen Hadfield, wrote a letter and spoke about her concerns regarding the language in the staff report. County Attorney Jeff Gore clarified that the only legal document that is relevant is the special exception permit which lists several conditions. A staff report is not part of what is being approved. Mr. Gore stated that this vote would be to allow this property to be used assembly hall under the ordinance. o The Chairman of the Planning Commission, Larkin Moyer, spoke in favor of the permit on behalf of the Planning Commission. o Chairman Felts closed the Public Hearing. o Supervisor Easter made a motion to approve the Special Exception Permit request to allow an “Assembly Hall” use to be conducted on the property as proposed with the following conditions as noted. Motion was approved unanimously. 3 BOARD MEMBERS’ COMMENTS/REPORTS District 1-The Honorable David M. Felts o Attended Piedmont Regional Jail meeting; 56 residents in July. o Powhatan Motorsports Parkway request was denied last night at meeting. District 2-The Honorable Dexter Jones o Attended PSR, CRC and VACOR meetings. District 3-The Honorable Benjamin Morris o Ameila County Fair was a good event. o Welcome back to school. o 9/11 Memorial event; look forward to attending. District 4-The Honorable Joseph Easter o Amelia County Fair was a great event & was appreciative of everyone that contributed. o Looking forward to upcoming events in the county. District 5-The Honorable Todd Robinson o Attended CPMT meeting. MOTION TO ADJOURN/CONTINUE MEETING o Supervisor Morris made a motion to adjourn August 26, 2026, regular meeting at 8:42 p.m. Motion was approved unanimously. BOTETOURT COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS MINUTES OF AUGUST 25, 2026 The Regular meeting of the Botetourt County Board of Supervisors was held on August 25, 2026, at the Botetourt County Administration Center, 57 S. Center Drive, Daleville, Virginia. PRESENT: Dr. Donald M. Scothorn, Chair, Valley District Mr. Brandon W. Nicely, Vice Chair, Fincastle District Mr. Tim Snyder, Amsterdam District Mr. Walter G. Michael, Blue Ridge District Ms. Linda Rottman, Buchanan District OTHERS PRESENT: Mr. Mike Lockaby, County Attorney Mr. Gary Larrowe, County Administrator/Clerk Mr. David Moorman, Deputy County Administrator Ms. Celeste Parker, Deputy Clerk Dr. Scothorn called the meeting to order at 12:33. On motion by Mr. Michael, seconded by Mr. Nicely, the Board went into Closed Session: • • • Subsection (A)(1) Discussion, consideration, or interviews of prospective candidates for employment; assignment, appointment, promotion, performance, demotion, salaries, disciplining, or resignation of specific public officers, appointees, or employees of any public body. Subsection (A)(3) Discussion or consideration of the acquisition of real property for a public purpose, or of the disposition of publicly held real property in the Blue Ridge, Buchanan and Valley Districts, where discussion in an open meeting would adversely affect the bargaining position or negotiating strategy of the public body. Subsection (A)(8) Consultation with legal counsel employed or retained by a public body regarding specific legal matters requiring the provision of legal advice by such counsel. MOTION: That the Board go into closed session. MOTION: Mr. Michael SECOND: Mr. Nicely AYES: Mr. Snyder, Mr. Michael, Dr. Scothorn, Mr. Nicely, Ms. Rottman RESOLUTION #26-08-01 At 1:59 p.m. Dr. Scothorn called the meeting to order and invited Supervisor Linda Rottman to lead the Pledge of Allegiance. Dr. Scothorn indicated that Mr. Moorman needed to leave the meeting early and aske the board to consider reordering the agenda to accommodate this change. Motion to reorder the agenda was made by Supervisor Michael and seconded by Supervisor Snyder. The motion carried unanimously. MOTION: To reorder the agenda, placing item #13 – Eagle Rock Property Cleanup immediately following the Consent Agenda. MOTION: Mr. Michael SECOND: Mr. Snyder AYES: Ms. Rottman, Mr. Nicely, Dr. Scothorn, Mr. Michael, Mr. Snyder RESOLUTION #: 26-08-02 Dr. Scothorn asked for a moment of silence. On a motion from Dr. Scothorn, seconded by Ms. Rottman, the Board returned to Regular Session from Closed Session. MOTION: That the Board return to regular session. MOTION: Dr. Scothorn SECOND: Ms. Rottman AYES: Mr. Snyder, Mr. Michael, Mr. Nicely, Ms. Rottman, Dr. Scothorn RESOLUTION #: 26-08-03 On motion by Mr. Michael, seconded by Mr. Nicely, the board adopted the following resolution by roll-call vote. BE IT RESOLVED, that to the best of the Board members’ knowledge only public business matters lawfully exempt from open meeting requirements and only such matters as were identified in the motion to go into Closed Session were heard, discussed or considered during the Closed Session. MOTION: That the Board adopt the Closed Session certification. MOTION: Mr. Michael SECOND: Mr. Nicely AYES: Mr. Snyder, Mr. Michael, Mr. Nicely, Ms. Rottman, Dr. Scothorn RESOLUTION #26-08-04 PRESENTATION BY DELEGATE TERRY AUSTIN & COMMENDATION OF STEVE CLINTON Delegate Terry Austin (37th House District) provided an overview of legislative activity at the state level, touching on the following subjects: State Budget, Federal Funding Cuts, Data Centers, Interstate 81, and Constitutional Amendments. Delegate Austin then presented House Resolution No. 432, commending Stephen Parks Clinton for 23 years of service on the Botetourt County Board of Supervisors. The resolution, agreed to by the House of Delegates on March 13, 2026, recognized Mr. Clinton's engineering and finance background, military service as a Lieutenant Colonel in the U.S. Air Force, and his contributions to major capital projects including the Botetourt Sports Complex at Greenfield, the Botetourt-Craig Regional Jail, the Eagle Rock Library, and renovations to James River High School and Fincastle Library. Mr. Clinton accepted the commendation and offered remarks, reflecting on the importance of building quality staff and fostering an ethos of optimism and forward-looking economic development in Botetourt County. He credited the collective efforts of board members, administrators, and county employees for the county's progress. PUBLIC HEARING – BUDGET AMENDMENT PUBLIC HEARING Acting Finance Director Sweeney presented proposed amendments to the FY 2025–2026 budget. He explained that because the combined amendments exceed 1% of the total adopted budget expenditures, a public hearing is required under Section 15.2-2507 of the Code of Virginia. The proposed amendments to the 2026-2027 Botetourt County Budget in the amount of $36,086,313.00 as follows: a. $31,553,535.00 designated for specific purpose and/or restricted use for rollover of unspent funds. b. $4,422,139.00 for rollover of unspent funds. c. $4,000 for the Treasurer's Office for additional Convention/Education/Lodging and Subsistence Funds. d. $200 for Fire & EMS donations. e. 52,397 for Electoral Board/Registrar for the August Primary. f. $54,042 for the Jail, Dispatch and Sheriff’s Office accounts related to miscellaneous fees and reimbursements. Total amendment requested: $36,086,313. Supervisor Rottman asked for clarification on "proprietary funds" and confirmed that Items E and F include state reimbursements. She also inquired whether all items in Part B were already under contract or obligation; staff confirmed that the listed items, such as fire apparatus on order and the compactor replacement, represent existing purchase orders or active projects. Public Comment: Danny Goad, Valley District requested a breakdown of how the amendment funds are distributed across budget categories. He also raised broader concern about the growing gap between the county's adopted and final budgets, noting that the final budget often deviates substantially from the original without a clear explanation, and that audited expenditures tend to align more closely with the original budget. He requested that the finance department provide explanatory data. Motion to approve the proposed FY 2025–2026 budget amendments in the amount of $36,086,313 was made and seconded. The motion carried 4-1, Supervisor Rottman opposed. MOTION: That the Board approve the proposed FY 2025–2026 budget amendments in the amount of $36,086,313. MOTION: Mr. Snyder SECOND: Mr. Nicely AYES: Mr. Snyder, Mr. Nicely, Mr. Michael, Dr. Scothorn NAYS: Ms. Rottman RESOLUTION #26-08-05 VDOT MONTHLY UPDATE VDOT Representative Andrew Thorpe presented the monthly update: • • • • • • Resurfacing: The 2026 surface treatment contracts are underway countywide, with contractor completion scheduled for mid-November. All routes remain on schedule. Exit 162 (Route 11 south of Buchanan): Acceleration lane project ongoing; drainage and grading work active. I-81, Exits 143–150: Widening project to three lanes in each direction is progressing. Blasting of rock began this week and will continue Tuesday–Thursday, 9–11 AM, for approximately eight weeks, requiring slow rolls on I-81 during those times. Laymantown Road: Reopened on schedule before the start of the school year. Final cleanup items underway. Haymaker Town Road: Closed for bridge superstructure replacement through September 4th. Emergency access maintained; Fire, EMS, and schools were notified. Mowing and Maintenance: Primary route mowing is complete; secondary route mowing ongoing. Brush cutting, gravel road grading, pothole patching, and work order responses are active. Thorpe provided individual follow-up updates: • • • Supervisor Nicely: Wheatland Road ditch regrading is complete. Supervisor Rottman: Truck signage upgrades at Exit 168 are being planned for both northbound and southbound off-ramps to intercept trucks before entering Arcadia. A follow-up email was sent regarding trees on Wheatland Road. Supervisor Snyder: Dal-Nita Hills driveway drainage issue — VDOT will seek contact information for the property owner to explore simple corrective measures. Supervisor Nicely mentioned a concern regarding potholes on Red Bud Lane; VDOT will inspect. Supervisor Nicely expressed appreciation for the productive meeting with the Town of Fincastle. Supervisor Michael inquired about the bridge study; VDOT will check with the bridge crew. EAGLE ROCK PROPERTY CLEANUP Deputy County Administrator David Moorman provided an informational update on the cleanup of the county-owned blighted property at 72 Railroad Avenue, Eagle Rock. No action was requested. The county received a Virginia Department of Emergency Management (VDEM) Hazard Mitigation grant of $132,854 to acquire and clean up the lot. Seven bids were received, ranging from a low of $225,051 to a high of $883,959 — all exceeding available grant funds. Staff successfully negotiated with the state to reallocate grant funds to raise the available total to $180,444, still significantly below the low bid. Staff is engaged in two concurrent efforts: seeking additional grant funding and negotiating with the low bidder to reduce the project scope or cost. The original September 30, 2026 completion deadline was extended by 12 months to September 30, 2027. Supervisor Rottman noted that the budget amendment included a line item of $213,895 for the project and asked for clarification. Moorman explained that the total grant amount covers multiple eligible costs beyond physical cleanup — including surveying, title searches, and legal work — all of which are restricted to their designated purposes and cannot be redirected to cleanup expenses. Only $180,444 of the total can be applied to the physical remediation work. Supervisor Nicely asked why bids came in so high. Moorman cited inflationary escalation over the approximately two years between the original quotes (used for the grant application in 2023) and the current bidding period, as well as potential worst-case assumptions by contractors regarding asbestos and material disposal logistics. ROANOKE VALLEY COLLECTIVE RESPONSE REQUEST FOR INTERNATIONAL OVERDOSE AWARENESS DAY PROCLAMATION Deputy County Administrator David Moorman presented a request from the Roanoke Valley Collective Response, a program of the Roanoke Valley-Allegheny Regional Commission, to recognize August 31st as International Overdose Awareness Day. The theme for 2026 is "25 Years On, Still Needed." A regional observance was scheduled for the following evening at the Taubman Museum of Art in Roanoke. Supervisor Rottman asked whether adopting the proclamation created any financial obligation for the county; staff confirmed it did not. Motion to adopt the proclamation and authorize the Chair to sign on behalf of the full Board was made and seconded. The motion carried unanimously. MOTION: That the Board adopt the proclamation and authorize the Chair to sign on behalf of the full Board. He accommodated one speaker ahead of order due to a health issue. Please note that the citizen comment period was worked around timed agenda items. Multiple citizens addressed the Board during the comment period, Themes included the planning commission appointment, zero-based budgeting, concerns about the proposed Google data center (water resources, transparency, and NDAs), and calls for greater responsiveness to constituents. LAW OFFICE & HOTEL UPDATE Capital Projects Manager Rich Evans introduced the presentation, noting that conceptual design for the Breckenridge Law Office and Hotel Rebuild project is now complete. Allison Blanton (architectural historian) and Carter Smith (architect) from Hill Studio presented the findings. Historical Context and Process: The advisory committee worked through approximately five to six meetings to review the building's evolutionary history, identifying two significant periods: the circa-1790s Breckenridge Law Office and the mid-19th to early-20th century Western Hotel era. The committee agreed the 1790s law office section was the most historically significant element and warranted the most precise replication. Design Concept: Rather than attempting two standalone buildings — which was ruled out due to insufficient site area and budget — the committee directed a single building design that tells the architectural story of the building's evolution. The committee determined that a white box approach offers maximum flexibility for future use as the Fincastle downtown area continues to evolve. Preliminary construction industry consultations indicate the project can be built within the allocated budget. Delegate Austin was noted to be working with Colonial Williamsburg to potentially source period-accurate bricks. The Board thanked Hill Studio and the advisory committee for the presentation. No action was required. RVARC WATER STUDY UPDATE Jeremy Holmes, Executive Director of the Roanoke Valley-Alleghany Regional Commission (RVARC), presented an update on the state-mandated water supply planning process. Background: Virginia has required regional water supply planning since 2001. The first regional plan was adopted in 2013, with a data update in 2018. A new planning cycle was mandated in 2024, with a completion deadline of October 9, 2029. RVARC is leading the process for two Regional Planning Areas (RPAs): the Upper James (Botetourt, Craig, Alleghany County, and Covington — the primary RPA for Botetourt) and the Roanoke River (Roanoke Valley, Franklin, and Bedford). Scope: The plan requires inventory of current water use (community water systems, large selfsupplied users, local utilities), public engagement, technical modeling of future supply and demand, risk/gap identification, and recommendations. RVARC will lead the public engagement and inventory phases internally; technical modeling will require a third-party consultant. Funding Challenges: The state allocated $750,000 per year statewide, divided among approximately 39 planning units. RVARC receives approximately $80,000 per year for both RPAs combined. Estimated full plan costs range from $360,000 (Upper James) to $600,000 (Roanoke River). The primary funding strategy has been an application to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Technical Assistance Program, which would cover 100% of Upper James costs (no local match required) and 50% of Roanoke River costs. However, RVARC learned the prior week that the Corps has paused the awarding of new grants due to federal fiscal uncertainty. RVARC remains hopeful funding will resume after October. Next Steps: RVARC is continuing scoping and cost estimation work with the Corps. Options under consideration include seeking additional General Assembly appropriations, phasing work as funding allows, or requesting local contributions. A water supply planning website has been launched to document progress and provide public access to planning materials. Supervisor Rottman asked whether the Western Virginia Water Authority's independent water study could be leveraged to reduce regional plan costs. Mr. Holmes confirmed that any such studies would be incorporated to avoid redundant work. RVARC staff member Amanda clarified that the Authority's study covers only its own service area and will not fulfill the full regional mandate, but will be a valuable input. Page 3 of 36 PRESENT: Byron Adkins, Sr., Chairman Ryan Patterson, Vice Chairman Michael Hill, Board Member Keith C. Rogers, Jr., County Administrator Christina Crawley-Jones, Finance Director Opening and Procedural Matters RE: CALL TO ORDER/ROLL CALL/ PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE The Chairman, Mr. Adkins, Sr., formally called to order the August 25, 2026, Board of Supervisors meeting. The roll call was conducted by Ms. Crawley-Jones, and the Pledge of Allegiance was recited in unison by all present. RE: ADOPTION OF AGENDA/ APPROVAL OF BOARD MINUTES/AWARDS AND PRESENTATIONS Chairman Adkins asked for a motion to adopt the agenda. Agenda Adoption Vice-Chairman Patterson motioned to adopt the agenda. The motion went as follows: Mr. Ryan Patterson, aye Mr. Michael Hill, aye Mr. Byron Adkins, Sr., aye Approval of July 28, 2026, Meeting Minutes Vice-Chairman Patterson motioned to approve the meeting minutes. The motion went as follows: Mr. Ryan Patterson, aye Mr. Michael Hill, aye Mr. Byron Adkins, Sr., aye Awards and Presentations D. Proclamation: In Memory of the Honorable Floyd H. Miles Sr. Page 4 of 36 RE: BOARD APPOINTMENTS A. Colonial Community Criminal Justice Board – Jayson Crawley, Sheriff B. Colonial Community Criminal Justice Board – Tyler Klink, Commonwealth Attorney RE: CONSENT AGENDA None. RE: REGULAR AGENDA None. RE: PUBLIC COMMENT PERIOD Ms. Crawley-Jones read the disclosure for the public comment period, stating that individuals commenting would have three minutes each; as a group, they would have five minutes. Please name and identify your group by showing your hands or standing. Please state your name. You do not have to state your address. The Board does not answer questions nor establish dialogue during the Public Comment period. Please approach the podium when called, state your name, and any relevant facts or materials. Written comments and documents may be submitted for the record. Key Issues Raised by Citizens Lloyd Carter expressed concerns regarding unresolved wastewater treatment issues at the Ruthville facility and questioned why previously identified repairs and grant opportunities were not pursued. He also raised concerns about the lack of archaeological studies for approximately 4,437 acres approved for solar development near historic sites and burial grounds. Dorene Billingsly expressed concern about the lack of substantive items on the Board’s agenda despite citizens’ repeated requests for information. She called for improved financial reporting, limits on data center development, corrective action regarding the forensic audit and capital project overspending, and updates on the Comprehensive Plan. She urged the Board to increase transparency, engage in meaningful public dialogue, and address these concerns at upcoming meetings. Pat Davis Pat Davis expressed concern about the potential effects of data center development on Charles City County, citing Loudoun County’s experience as a cautionary example. She questioned whether the by-right designation limits County oversight and raised concerns about whether Point One had provided complete information regarding its proposed equipment and infrastructure. She urged the County to strengthen its regulations and remove data centers as a by-right use, noting that several Virginia localities have taken similar action. Brandi Marano, speaking on behalf of a group, emphasized the importance of accountability, transparency, responsible spending, and public trust in County government. She urged County leaders to improve communication, meaningfully engage residents, consistently apply policies, evaluate long-term financial and infrastructure impacts, and ensure that decisions regarding growth and development align with the County’s goals and serve the public interest. Jared Kline expressed agreement with concerns regarding the limited agenda and information provided. He Page 5 of 36 encouraged the Board and County administration to include more substantive topics, provide updates on ongoing County initiatives, and use future meetings to demonstrate progress and promote productive public engagement. Preston Adkins thanked the County for holding the recent workshop and requested that future discussions with Waste Management focus on landfill operations in Charles City County rather than recycling operations located elsewhere. He also renewed his request for an oversight committee for the paid fire department and raised concerns about vehicle use, fuel costs, traffic control, safety, and potential liability during emergency responses. Bill Hopke expressed concern about unresolved questions identified in the court-ordered forensic audit, particularly missing documentation and the County’s inability to explain or reconcile certain expenditures involving public funds. He commended Finance Director Christina Crawley-Jones for assisting the auditors and providing testimony despite not being employed by the County during most of the period reviewed. He asked the Board to publicly identify all material unanswered questions and explain the steps that will be taken to address them. Thelma Whitehead provided an update regarding assistance for Ms. Jones, thanking Kathy Brown and other community members for helping secure a wheelchair ramp and arrange replacement windows. She also expressed disappointment with the forensic audit’s outcome but encouraged citizens to remain engaged and vote. Additionally, she questioned the level of support shown by County leadership for the Finance Director during the court proceedings. David Ware reflected on Virginia history and emphasized the principles of equality, representation, and accountable government. He expressed concern that his district lacked representation on the Charles City Planning Commission while other districts had multiple members. He questioned the fairness of the appointments and called for Chairman Adkins to resign. Martha Harris, speaking on behalf of a group, expressed dissatisfaction with the forensic audit’s findings and the Board’s response. She questioned why the Board had not initiated the audit or ensured that auditors received complete documentation, particularly credit card records. She urged the Board and citizens to continue seeking verifiable information, accountability, and a full explanation of how County funds were spent. Jackie Stewart emphasized citizens continued focus on County finances, debt, wastewater improvements, groundwater protection, data center permitting, and environmental oversight. Drawing on nearly 30 years of local and regional government experience, she encouraged open government, responsible spending, measurable planning, and collaboration between citizens and County leaders. She offered to work with the County to develop practical solutions and move these priorities forward. The county is working to make applications and permits more available online. Reports from prior fiscal years have been moved to the archive section of the Financial Reports webpage. THE HONORABLE RYAN PATTERSON THE HONORABLE MICHAEL HILL COMMONWEALTH OF VIRGINIA COUNTY of CHARLES CITY Proclamation A PROCLAMATION DECLARING OCTOBER AS DOMESTIC VIOLENCE AWARENESS MONTH WHEREAS, domestic violence is a serious crime that affects people of all races, ages, gender, and income levels; and WHEREAS, domestic violence is widespread and affects over four million Americans each year; and WHEREAS, one in three Americans have witnessed an incident of domestic violence; and WHEREAS, children that grow up in violent homes are believed to be abused and neglected at a rate higher than the national average; and WHEREAS, domestic violence costs the nation billions of dollars annually in medical expenses, police and court costs, shelters, foster care, sick leave, absenteeism, and non- productivity; and WHEREAS, only a coordinated community effort will put a stop to this heinous crime; and. WHEREAS, Domestic Violence Awareness Month provides an excellent opportunity for citizens to learn more about preventing domestic violence and to show support for the numerous organizations and individuals who provide critical advocacy, services, and assistance to victims. NOW, THEREFORE, IT IS PROCLAIMED by the Charles City County Board of Supervisors the month of October as Domestic Violence Awareness Month and ask the citizens of Charles City County to work together to eliminate domestic violence from our community. Proclaimed this 22 day of September, 2026, by the Board of Supervisors of Charles City, Virginia. County of Charles City Board of Supervisors Page 10 of 36 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS THE HONORABLE BYRON ADKINS SR. THE HONORABLE RYAN PATTERSON THE HONORABLE MICHAEL HILL COMMONWEALTH OF VIRGINIA COUNTY of CHARLES CITY Proclamation HONORING JOEL MILLER FOR BRAVERY AND HEROISM WHEREAS, Charles City County recognizes the courage, compassion, and willingness to assist others demonstrated by individuals who place the safety and well-being of others above their own; and WHEREAS, Joel Miller demonstrated extraordinary bravery and selflessness when an individual entered the river and was in need of immediate assistance; and WHEREAS, recognizing the seriousness of the situation, Mr. Miller did not hesitate to respond. Utilizing a canoe, he paddled out into the river toward the individual in distress; and WHEREAS, Mr. Miller successfully reached the individual, provided assistance, and helped bring the person safely back toward the shoreline, where emergency personnel were standing by to provide additional assistance and medical care; and WHEREAS, Mr. Miller's actions exemplify the highest ideals of courage, compassion, and service to others. His willingness to act during a potentially dangerous and life-threatening situation contributed significantly to the successful rescue; and WHEREAS, The actions of citizens such as Mr. Miller demonstrate the important role that individuals can play in protecting and preserving the lives of others within our community; and WHEREAS, the Board of Supervisors of Charles City County desires to formally recognize and commend Joel Miller for his courageous actions and his commitment to helping another person in a time of great need. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT PROCLAIMED, that the Charles City County Board of Supervisors, on behalf of the citizens of Charles City County, hereby recognizes and honors Joel Miller for his exceptional bravery, courage, and selfless actions in assisting with the rescue of an individual from the river. His actions reflect great credit upon himself and serve as an outstanding example of courage, compassion, and community spirit. BE IT FURTHER PROCLAIMED, that Charles City County extends its sincere appreciation to Joel Miller for his willingness to place himself in harm's way to assist another person and for demonstrating the values of courage, service, and humanity that make our community stronger. (City Code sec.2-71) • Remarks and actions that disrupt the progress of the Council meeting, and remarks from persons other than councilors, the City Manager, the City Attorney, or a presenter for an Agenda Item are not permitted. • The presiding officer shall call an individual to order, including a councilor, when that individual goes afoul of these rules. The following are examples of remarks and behavior that are not permitted: • i. Interrupting a speaker who is addressing Council at the speaker's microphone, or interrupting a speaker who has otherwise been invited to address Council during Community Matters or a Public Hearing ii. Interrupting a councilor who is speaking iii. Shouting, and talking (either individually or in concert with others) in a manner that prevents a speaker or a Councilor from being heard or that otherwise hinders the progress of the meeting iv. Blocking paths for emergency exit from the meeting room; engaging in any conduct that prevents a member of the audience from seeing or hearing councilors during a meeting; standing on chairs or tables within the Council meeting room v. Threats or incitement of violence toward councilors, City staff or members of the public vi. Engaging in conduct that is a criminal offense under the City Code or the Virginia Code vii. Campaigning for elected office viii. Promotion of private business ventures ix. Using profanity or vulgarity x. Personal attacks against Councilors, City staff or members of the public xi. Behavior which tends to intimidate others During a City Council meeting the presiding officer shall have control of the Council Chambers and the connecting halls and corridors within City Hall, and any other venue where a Council meeting is being held. In case of any conduct described above, the presiding officer may take measures deemed appropriate, including but not limited to suspending the meeting until order is restored, ordering areas to be cleared by the Sergeant at Arms, or requiring any individual to exit the meeting room and adjacent premises (connecting halls and corridors.)

text: Special Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council Board of Directors Meeting Municipal Building, 300 N Main Street Hopewell Council Chambers September 29, 2026 5:00 p.m. AGENDA 1. Call To Order 2. Introduction of Joint Meeting Agenda and Purpose: Charles J. Bennett, Director of Economic Development and Tourism Report 3. New Business a. The Role of the Hopewell EDA: Powers, Accomplishments, and Future Direction b. Business Recruitment and Retention: Targets, Tools, Tactics, and Incentives c. Priority Redevelopment Areas & Investment Strategy d. Strategic Property Acquisition and Blight Removal Fund e. Proposal to develop a Vision Plan for a new gateway district 4. Closed Meeting: Suggested Motion: To hold a closed meeting to discuss (a) the acquisition of real property for a public purpose where discussion in an open meeting would adversely affect the bargaining position or negotiating strategy of the public body, pursuant to Virginia Code § 2.2-3711(A)(3) (Potential acquisition of property, Support agreement with City Council on transaction of property) and (b) consultation with legal counsel employed or retained by a public body regarding specific legal matter requiring legal advice, pursuant to Virginia Code § 2.23711(A)(8). (certain key riverfront and downtown area properties) Adjournment Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 1. Page 1 of 40 Call To Order Role call by Staff to confirm members for quorum for both Hopewell Economic Development Authority, and Hopewell City Council. 2. Introduction of Joint Meeting Agenda and Purpose: Charles J. Bennett, Director of Economic Development and Tourism Report Good evening, Mayor, members of City Council, members of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority, and members of City staff and public Thank you for joining us for this special joint meeting. I would also like to welcome Ms. Lisa Wilson, Director of the Hopewell Redevelopment and Housing Authority, who is joining us this evening. The purpose of tonight’s meeting is straightforward: to bring City Council and the Economic Development Authority together so that we are working in sync around Hopewell’s economic-development priorities. Tonight gives us an opportunity to look back and celebrate the progress we have made, to look forward with vision, and to discuss the tools and tactics that we can use together to turn that vision into results. This conversation does not begin with a blank sheet of paper. In early 2025, City Council and the Economic Development Authority adopted the City of Hopewell Economic Development Strategic Plan for 2024 through 2034. That plan was developed through a collaborative process involving the EDA, City Council representatives, City staff, and community stakeholders. The plan was intended to serve as a road map for Hopewell’s future. It recognizes that human development, community development, housing, tourism, redevelopment, and traditional economic development are interconnected. As the plan explains, when our organizations work from the same strategy, we are much more likely to arrive at the same destination: a thriving, diverse, prosperous, and safe community. Tonight is an opportunity to reconnect our work to that adopted plan. Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 Page 2 of 40 The plan identifies several major areas of focus, including our business corridors, Historic Downtown, the riverfront, housing, tourism and history, health care, and our industrial and manufacturing base. It also identifies specific redevelopment opportunities, including Cavalier Square, Downtown Hopewell, and the marina and Appomattox River waterfront. These are ambitious goals. Accomplishing them will require more than any one organization acting independently. City Council establishes the community’s broader vision, policies, and funding priorities. The EDA provides specialized economic-development tools that can help attract investment, support businesses, finance projects, and acquire or reposition strategic properties. The Hopewell Redevelopment and Housing Authority brings another important set of capabilities to this partnership. Its mission and statutory role are focused on housing, neighborhood revitalization, redevelopment, and addressing blighted or underutilized properties. Depending upon the project and the required approvals, the Authority can participate in redevelopment planning, acquire and rehabilitate property, pursue housing resources, and work with public and private partners to implement redevelopment projects. That role may be especially valuable as we move forward with mixed-use projects such as Cavalier Square. Our strategic plan envisions Cavalier Square as a modern mixed-use development combining business and retail activity with affordable housing, market-rate housing, and lifestyle and recreational amenities. Achieving that vision will require us to coordinate economic development, housing, infrastructure, planning, private investment, and community needs. Director Wilson, we appreciate your being here and look forward to strengthening the working relationship among the Housing Authority, the EDA, City Council, and City staff. As we move through tonight’s agenda, I hope we will keep several questions in mind: What kind of Hopewell are we working to create? What investments and redevelopment opportunities should receive our greatest attention? What barriers are keeping important projects from moving forward? Which organization has the right tool to address each barrier? Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 Page 3 of 40 And how can we coordinate our resources so that public participation produces measurable private investment and lasting community benefit? Tonight is not intended to resolve every issue or approve every future project. It is an opportunity to build a shared understanding, establish direction, and make sure that City Council, the EDA, the Housing Authority, and staff are moving forward as partners. We have accomplished important things together, and we should celebrate those successes. At the same time, we have an opportunity to become more intentional, more proactive, and more strategic about Hopewell’s future. If we remain aligned around the vision established in our strategic plan—and if we use each organization’s tools wisely—we can continue moving Hopewell from opportunity to investment and from vision to implementation. Thank you again for being here. With that, I would like to move us into the first portion of tonight’s discussion: the role of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority, its accomplishments, and its future direction. This next part of the presentation will be made by: Kyle English, Business Retention & Expansion Specialist, External Relations Officer. Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 Page 4 of 40 3.a The Role of the Hopewell EDA: Power, Accomplishments, and Future Direction Purpose The Hopewell Economic Development Authority is a separate political subdivision that provides the City with tools and flexibility to advance economic development initiatives. While City Council establishes broader community priorities and policy direction, the EDA can serve as an implementation partner by facilitating business investment, redevelopment, financing, property transactions and other economic development activities. Why an EDA Matters The EDA's role is considerably broader than business incentives. Among its authorized purposes are assisting businesses with acquiring, owning, leasing or disposing of property and provide financing through loans and/or grants to promote industry and trade. Its purposes can also extend to industrial parks, governmental facilities, certain nonprofit facilities, medical facilities, infrastructure and other eligible projects. The EDA as a Tool of City Council The Hopewell Economic Development Authority provides a mechanism for translating the City's economic development priorities into actionable projects. City Council and the EDA have distinct roles, but their efforts can be aligned around shared economic development goals. Council helps establish the City's broader vision, priorities and desired outcomes. Economic Development staff then work to identify strategies, projects and opportunities that advance those priorities. The EDA provides specialized tools that can be deployed to help move those opportunities from concept to implementation. Council Priority → Economic Development Strategy → EDA Tool → Private/Public Investment → Community Impact Council Priority Increase inventory or market-ready properties Revitalize an underutilized commercial area Potential Strategy Address barriers preventing development Assemble or reposition key properties Potential EDA Role Site preparation, infrastructure, property activation Acquire, hold, improve, or convey property Intended Outcome More competitive business recruitment sites Redevelopment and new private investment Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 Page 5 of 40 What Tools Are Available? Tool How it can Advance Hopewell’s Priorities Property Acquisition & Redevelopment Business & Property Financing Performance-Based Incentives Site Readiness & Infrastructure Develop Partnerships Acquire, hold, improve, lease, or convey strategic properties to facilitate redevelopment, address barriers to investment and position sites for productive private use. Provide loans or other eligible financial assistance to help businesses expand, activate commercial properties, and address financing gaps that may prevent private investment. Support business attraction, retention and expansion through assistance tied to measurable outcomes such as capital investment, job creation/retention, wages and development. Support site preparation, infrastructure and other improvements necessary to make properties more competitive for private investment and business recruitment. Work with the City, property owners, businesses, developers, and outside partners to structure projects and leverage public resources to generate greater private investment. Serve as a financing vehicle for eligible economic development and governmental capital projects, including property acquisition, infrastructure, and other public investments. Capital Financing Using the Tools Strategically The appropriate EDA tool will vary from project to project. The starting point should be the economic development objective, followed by an assessment of the specific barrier preventing that objective from being achieved. Priority  Barrier  EDA Tool  Investment  Impact What do we want to accomplish? → What is standing in the way? → Which EDA tool can help? → How can we leverage additional investment? → What public benefit will result? The tool should follow the objective—not the other way around. Effective use of the EDA begins with a clearly defined economic development priority and uses the Authority's powers strategically to address barriers, leverage investment and produce measurable community benefit. Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 Page 6 of 40 Economic incentives are tied to a public purpose and clear, quantifiable measures such as jobs, wages and investment, with appropriate performance protections. The same philosophy can apply more broadly: EDA activity should be driven by the outcome Hopewell is trying to achieve. Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 Page 7 of 40 The EDA at Work: Turning Tools into Results The Hopewell EDA has supported business investment, redevelopment, and business growth through a variety of projects and financial tools. More recently, the City and EDA have worked to establish a more intentional set of programs designed to address specific barriers to investment in Hopewell. These programs demonstrate the approach outlined on the previous pages: identify the barrier, select the appropriate tool, and use EDA resources strategically to help generate private investment and community benefit. Building Hopewell’s Economic Development Toolbox Program Barrier Addressed Hopewell Sites Ready Vacant and underutilized commercial properties Marketing Program may lack visibility and exposure to prospective businesses, developers, and site selectors. Legacy Business Existing businesses can face financial barriers to Grant Program reinvesting in aging properties, completing improvements, or expanding operations. Invest Hopewell Business Loan Program Businesses and prospective investors may encounter financing gaps that cannot be fully addressed through conventional lending. Sites Ready Property Activation Loan Program A property may have redevelopment potential but require improvements before it can realistically be marketed or occupied. How the Tool Responds Partners with property owners to identify and actively market available sites and buildings through City economic development channels and direct outreach. Provides matching reimbursement assistance of up to $10,000 to eligible established Hopewell businesses, encouraging private reinvestment and improvement of commercial properties. Provides an EDA financing option intended to supplement – not replace – conventional financing and help viable business investment and expansion projects move forward. Provides property owners and developers an opportunity to seek EDA financing for improvements that help activate properties and position them for investment. The Takeaway Hopewell is quickly moving toward a more proactive EDA model, building tools that address known barriers to investment before an individual project or prospect requires them. Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 Page 8 of 40 Examples of the EDA at Work Stone’s Diner Parking Lot Project – EDA provided financing to Stone’s Diner complete repair and replacement of their parking lot. Boathouse Project – EDA obtained financing to transform the former Navigator’s Den to the Boathouse Restaurant City Point Ice Cream and Burgers Expansion Project – EDA provided financing for the rehabilitation of 238 E Broadway to house the expanded City Point Ice Cream and Burgers. 7-Brew Attraction – EDA is acting as conduit for grant approved by City Council for the removal the former Denny’s building. Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 Page 9 of 40 Future Direction – Using the EDA Strategically The EDA can and will continue responding to individual business and development opportunities as they arise, but its powers also provide an opportunity for a more proactive and strategic approach, one in which City Council and the EDA identify shared economic development priorities and intentionally align resources, programs, and investment around those priorities. Moving from Transactional to Strategic Going forward, the opportunity is to use the EDA not only to respond to individual projects, but also to anticipate barriers, invest in opportunities and create the conditions necessary for private investment. Four Strategic Directions 1. Be more proactive with strategic property – Identify properties that are important to Hopewell’s economic development objectives and determine where EDA involvement could help unlock their potential. This could include acquiring or controlling strategic properties, addressing redevelopment barriers, assembling sites, improving marketability, or positioning properties for future private investment. a. Desired outcome: Move key properties from underutilized to investment-ready. 2. Invest in readiness, not just recruitment - Successful recruitment depends on having competitive properties and infrastructure available when opportunities arise. The EDA can help Hopewell address site-readiness barriers before a prospect is at the table, including property conditions, infrastructure, site preparation and other improvements that affect a site's competitiveness. a. Desired outcome: Move from having available property to having competitive development opportunities. 3. Build Sustainable Economic Development Resources - Continue developing financing and investment tools that allow EDA resources to be reused and leveraged over time. Revolving loan programs, property activation financing and other structured investments can help address financing gaps while allowing repayments to support future projects. a. Desired outcome: Move from one-time assistance toward recycling economic development capital. 4. Leverage Partnerships to Increase Impact - The EDA does not have to accomplish economic development objectives alone. Its greatest impact may occur when EDA participation helps bring together City resources, private capital, developers, property owners, financial institutions and state or federal partners. The objective should be to use public participation strategically where it can help unlock or accelerate greater private investment. a. Desired outcome: Use targeted public participation to generate greater overall investment and community benefit. Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 Page 10 of 40 Discussion: We understand the EDA’s role, we know the tools available, and we’re already building programs around them. So how can Council and the EDA most effectively use the Authority’s powers to advance Hopewell’s economic development priorities? Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 Page 11 of 40 3.b Business Recruitment and Retention: Targets, Tools, Tactics, and Incentives How Business Recruitment Works Business Recruitment is rarely a single interaction. Prospects may originate through direct outreach, state/regional partners, commercial real estate relationships, developers, existing businesses, site-selection inquiries, or businesses that independently express interest in Hopewell. The role of Economic Development is to move these opportunities through a coordinated process – from identifying a prospect to finding the right location, addressing barriers, assembling resources, and securing investment in Hopewell. The Recruitment Process Generate Prospect  Understand Project  Match Opportunity  Identify Barrier  Assemble Response  Compete for Investment Recruitment is a Team Effort Hopewell’s recruitment efforts can involve coordination among the City, EDA, property owners, developers, commercial real estate professionals, utilities, financial institutions, and state/regional economic development partners. The City’s role is to make it as easy as reasonably possible for a qualified prospect to answer three questions: 1. Can my project work here? 2. Can Hopewell meet my timeline? 3. Does Hopewell provide a competitive business environment for this investment? Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 Page 12 of 40 Joint Meeting of the Hopewell Economic Development Authority and City Council 9/29/2026 Page 13 of 40 How Hopewell Competes Recruitment requires more than incentives. Hopewell’s competitiveness depends on its ability to combine its inherent advantages with the appropriate economic development tools for each project. Real Estate & Site Readiness -Available buildings, sites, & land -Property ID and owner engagement -Sites Ready Marketing Program -Property Activation -Site prep and infrastructure Objective: Give prospects viable locations that can meet their requirements and timelines. Financing & Incentives -EDA financing -Invest Hopewell Business Loan Program -Performance-based local incentives -Virginia Enterprise Zone tools -State incentive programs Objective: … Potential Targets Investment Type Manufacturing and Industrial, Micro Data Centers, Green Energy Downtown & Small Business Retail & Restaurants Hospitality & Tourism Housing/Mixed-Use Emerging Industries Potential Economic Development

(d.) Priority for comments is given to City residents, taxpayers, and business owners.(e.) Speakers may not yield time. (f.) Groups of speakers on the same topic must designate a single representative. Comments violating these rules may not be presented at the Council meeting. (g.) This policy does not apply to public hearings, at which any citizen of Martinsville may appear and speak on the subject of the public hearing. a. 9. text: City of Radford Planning Commission Agenda September 21, 2026 10 Robertson St., Radford, VA 6:00pm. – Regular Meeting Call to order Determination of a quorum Approval of Agenda Approval of Minutes: August 17, 2026 – Regular Meeting CITIZEN COMMENTS ON PUBLIC MATTERS: (Please state your name for the record – Please limit comments to 3 minutes or less) 1. Work Session – Zoning Ordinance Update Staff Report Planning Commission Member Comments Adjournment Future Meetings October 5, 2026 TBD October 19, 2026 -6:00 pm Regular Meeting City of Radford, Virginia • 10 Robertson Street • Radford, Virginia 24141 • Phone (540) 731-3603 • Fax (540) 731-3699 • www.radfordva.gov Radford Planning Commission Monday, August 17, 2026 Municipal Building Members Present: Mr. Castleberry Mr. Collier, Vice Chairperson Mr. Gropman Dr. Rzigalinski Dr. Pearce Mr. Watson, Chairperson Absent: Mr. Gillespie Staff/Visitors: Melissa Skelton, City Staff Mr. Watson called the meeting to order at 6:06 pm in the Radford City Council Chambers at 10 Robertson Street, Radford Virginia. A quorum was present. Approval of Agenda: Mr. Watson approved the agenda. Voting Yes: Mr. Castleberry, Mr. Collier, Mr. Gropman, Dr. Pearce, Dr. Rzigalinski, Mr. Watson Approval of Minutes for July 20, 2026: Minutes were recommended for approval as submitted by Mr. Castleberry, seconded by Dr. Rzigalinski. Voting Yes: Mr. Castleberry, Mr. Collier, Mr. Gropman, Dr. Pearce, Dr. Rzigalinski Voting No: None Abstain: Mr. Watson PUBLIC COMMENTS – No public comments were provided, since no public was in attendance. SUBJECT: Work Session Zoning Ordinance Commissioners discussed the draft ordinance: How family is defined; how is it used in the draft code; enforcement challenges. “Family” is used as a common term to refer to housing types; its use as a legal test is different. Additional search for precedent that might work in our situation. Maybe there are different ways to address the problem besides nuisance and family relationships. PID – make consistent with PUD. List kerosene with gas stations. Livestock still says “pleasure” – find a better definition. Difference between livestock and domesticated animals. B-3 central – “developing historical downtown” – will that preclude people from thinking of other areas in B-3 that aren’t historical? Could it be a hindrance for potential developers? Melissa - We don’t have an architectural/historic review board, so we wouldn’t impose constraints as a city. The developer would have to be pursuing tax credits. Medical arts – life care is listed twice. Chickens – follow state health department guidelines promptly; get rid of “extermination” as stated. Homestays – weren’t we going to distinguish what could happen in the business districts? How could we limit in the business district (and do we want to)? It presently says “no limitations”. Consider referring to the state regulations/codes on this. What part of the code might cover hostels/second floor individual units with no kitchens? Definitions in B-1: conflicting definitions of “basement” and what counts as a story – see Bart’s comments sent in a document around 5. Under “duplexes”, mixed in stuff about townhouses. R-4 setbacks have been increased from 6 to 10 for duplexes. Did we mean to do this? 126.56 under R-4. Double-check correctness. Duplex min lot size for R3 vs. R4. Townhouse lot size min 1600 sf? Please review. Different family daycare uses – governed by state law. Five or above vs. less (family matters here – you don’t have to count your own kids) “Educational facility” definition Review listed uses in a MHP – not all “ideal” Max accessory building size in MHP = 50%? Reduce minimum lot within R-4 to 75 from 80 (or to 40 from 50)? This was discussed but not implemented. Non-conforming lots – would have to go to the zoning board of appeals on a hardship basis. (This term doesn’t appear to be used in the draft code; is there a process that we can note or is it just word of mouth?). – Ask what Aphi’s answer to this is. Find out what Aphi’s answer was. How can we adjust this to promote growth and allow development of non-conforming lots? Duplexes – two 40’ houses on an 80’ lot? You can build detached houses but not duplexes given how it’s worded. Grandfathering 40’ lots? Subdivision rules? What was Aphi’s fix for 15’/20’ lots? Those are only buildable if you have a bunch of them together. We want to encourage infill. STAFF REPORT – Next work session is on Labor Day. Aphi would be available at our next regular meeting (Sept 21) for a work session. COMMISSION MEMBER COMMENTS Mr. Castleberry – appreciate everyone’s contributions! Mr. Collier – shared the same sentiment. Mr. Gillespie – Absent Mr. Gropman – appreciated the discussion Dr. Pearce – glad to see the ordinance “coming in for a landing”. Dr. Rzigalinski – me too. Mr. Watson – same A motion was made by Mr. Collier to adjourn the meeting at 7:39 pm, seconded by Dr. Rzigalinski. Voting Yes: Mr. Castleberry, Mr. Collier, Mr. Gropman, Dr. Pearce, Dr. Rzigalinski, Mr. Watson Voting No: None Submitted by: Annie R. Pearce, Secretary Date: August 17, 2026

The Mayor of the City, Raymond David Horton, was present and presiding. Other members of City Council present were, Vice-Mayor Seth Gillespie, Mrs. Kellie Artrip, Mrs. Foster and Mr. Guy Wohlford. Others present were as follows: Mr. Todd Meredith, City Manager Ms. Melissa Skelton, City Clerk ae Mrs. Patricia Cox, CFO MINUTES APPROVAL: Mr. Gillespie made a motion to approve the minutes of July 13,2026, July 22, 2026 and August 10, 2026, Mrs. Foster seconded the motion. VOTE: AYES: Mrs. Artrip, Mrs. Foster, Mr. Gillespie, Mr. Wohlford, Mayor Horton NAYES: NONE-O “aa CITIZEN COMMENTS: 4 Sean Whiteside describes difficulties getting approval from Radford City for solar energy. He shared that their original application in 2025 was denied, and they were restricted to a much smaller system (10 kW AC rather than the typical 25 kW allowed in Virginia), without clear explanation from city staff. He stated after installing the reduced system, they routinely produced surplus electricity, but the city kept the excess power for free while charging them monthly fees. He argued that these policies penalize solar customers despite their contributions to reducing strain on the grid during peak demand. He expressed concern that the city's approach discourages environmentally conscious residents, increases future costs related to health and infrastructure, and puts the community at risk during heat waves. He urges the city to revise its solar policies, allow larger systems, and fairly compensate residents who generate solar power. Dr. Joyce, Radford City School Superintendent, came this evening to urge Radford citizens to rely on accurate information when deciding on the upcoming 1% sales tax referendum. He explained that Radford has aging school facilities requiring ongoing maintenance, and the proposed tax would create a dedicated funding source to address these needs. Because the sales tax applies to all purchases made in the city—including visitors, tourists, and university students, it would generate an estimated $1.6 million annually without placing the entire burden on Radford residents. He noted that raising the same amount through property taxes would require a substantial increase that only local property owners would pay. Using sales tax revenue for school facilities would also free other local funds for projects like sidewalks, playgrounds, and outdoor learning spaces. He clarified that while Virginia Lottery proceeds support public education, they are insufficient to cover major construction or renovation needs and are spread across 131 school divisions. He emphasized that the 1% sales tax would be a locally controlled funding source dedicated solely to Radford City Schools and encourage residents to learn the facts, ask questions, and vote thoughtfully in November, and offer himself as a resource for anyone seeking more information. Keith Welton, a Radford property and business owner, expressed his support for the 1% sales tax because he feels its use is clearly defined. He shared his concern about the 212 Third Avenue project. He stated that when the project was previously reviewed, citizens and officials were unanimously against it, yet it continues moving forward. He stated that the shelter is already creating strain on the surrounding area and reported changes in where local children play and said people near his office have raised concerns. He describes increased public drug use near the site and claims that additional seating was added because too many individuals. were congregating in one place. He emphasizes that these issues are visible to anyone driving by and reiterates his belief that the project should not proceed. RECOGNITIONS: SUBJECT: VACP Valor Award Recipients SUMMARY: The Award for Valor recognizes a law enforcement officer who, in the line of duty, performs an act of extraordinary heroism while engaged with an adversary at imminent personal risk. On September 1, 2026, the Virginia Association of Chiefs of Police & Foundation (VACP) recognized twenty-six Virginia law enforcement officers from nine agencies with the Association's highest honor, the Award for Valor. Radford City Police Department had 3 officers who were recognized. Lieutenant Evan S. McManus, Sergeant Jordan Ellis and Officer Jacob Caudell. REPORT: Flock Camera’s - Chief Holdaway Chief Holdaway provided clarifications about how Flock safety cameras work after his previous discussion at councils previous meeting. He explained that Flock cameras do not track vehicles throughout the city, that they only capturing still images of cars passing specific intersections, including the vehicle’s color, make, model, and rear license plate. The system does not use facial recognition, Bluetooth collection, or other personal data technologies. Radford City Police fully own the data, keep it for 21 days, and delete it afterward. The cameras do not issue tickets or generate revenue. He referenced two recent Virginia court cases affirming that Flock data collection is constitutional and does not require search warrants. They emphasize that Virginia has strict rules preventing use of this data for federal, immigration, or reproductive rights enforcement and that it is used only for legitimate criminal justice purposes, such as locating wanted individuals or missing persons. The department audits the system monthly, follows high accreditation standards, and publishes its policies and transparency information online. The speaker also notes recent public discussion at the state level: the governor has expressed openness to limits on license plate technology but does not support an outright ban. They highlight Flock’s effectiveness, sharing a recent success in which camera data helped police quickly identify and arrest a suspect in a murder case. Finally, they recommend presenting Flock information to the Chief’s Advisory Panel—made up of local residents and business stakeholders—to gather community input and keep the public informed. Mayor Horton it was great to have a Chiefs Advisory group. He asked the Chief to confirm that for someone to access this data they have to have an identifier and case number. Chief Holdaway confirmed that they did and stated it was a Class 1 misdemeanor if you violate the policy Mr. Gillespie asked what was in place with our contract if we needed to shut this down. Chief responded that we could terminate the contract but would still have the associated costs. Mr. Wohlford asked if it was video or just a camera. Chief said it is just the rear of the car; they don’t see the driver. Mrs. Artrip asked if there are any other versions of Flock? Chief Holdaway responded that he could not speak on all the programs that Flock offered, but for us this is the version we use. Mrs. Artrip stated that this is what we're contracted to use and what the grant money was spent on. Mrs. Foster point out that the information Police Officers are pulling off the plate is the information they would pull off a plate during your routine stop. Chief Holdaway agreed and stated there is no more identifying information that they would typically run. PRESENTATIONS: SUBJECT: Mass Appraisal Firm for Reassessment — Vision Government Solutions SUMMARY: Vision Government Solutions has been recommended for the City of Radford’s 2028 Real Property Reassessment for mass appraisal of all real property within the city’s jurisdiction with values certified January 1, 2028. Mr. John Atkinson, Director of Sales, Vision Government Solutions, provided an overview of the Reassessment process that will be taking place. SUBJECT: Radford University Community Impact Report — Dr. Angela Joyner SUMMARY: Dr. Angela Joyner, Vice President for Economic and Community Development at Radford University, presented an overview of the Joint Commission’s work over the past year and the shared impact of university—city collaboration. She shared the Joint Commission worked on a strategic framework that is focused on economic development, community vibrancy, outdoor recreation and tourism, knowledge exchange, and collaborative governance. She shared that members of the commission have been working on the development of a comprehensive downtown retail strategy in partnership with the city, the chamber of commerce, and the New River Regional Commission. This work builds on previous studies and aims to strengthen business retention, attract new investment, and increase foot traffic. Public input is being gathered through surveys and a stakeholder session is scheduled for September 23. Placemaking initiatives were another highlight, including the opening of a pocket park at corner of Tyler and Main Streets, facade updates along East Main, and expanded access to Selu Conservancy. Planning continues for the Riverside Amphitheater, with programming development nearly complete and exploration underway of a future music festival as a pilot activation. Dr. Joyner reported that Community Fest has grown dramatically, expanding from over 2500 attendees last year to more than 5,000 this year, with 137 vendors and a new community performance stage. An economic impact study is being conducted to support future planning. She also detailed active collaboration on river stewardship, preparations for the Highlanders Festival, and outcomes from the inaugural Adventure Works Summit, which convened statewide partners to discuss outdoor recreation as an economic driver. The commission has also begun early discussions on converting the trestle near the Dedmon Center into a rails-to-trail connection with Pulaski County, identifying potential funding opportunities to support the project. She emphasized ongoing efforts to strengthen student engagement in the community through service initiatives, academic programming like the Wicked Festival, and continued Provost Talk sessions held at local businesses. Dr. Joyner provided updates included housing coordination for approximately 300 students seeking off-campus options, fiscal and enrollment updates from university leadership, and ongoing planning related to the university’s master plan and COGYN reinvestment. She closed by reaffirming the Joint Commission’s continued commitment to transparency, accountability, and partnership in advancing shared community goals. SUBJECT: AirMedCare Network SUMMARY: John Crocker of Air Medical Care Network (locally known as Lifeguard 10, 11, and 12) presented information regarding an air medical transport membership program available to municipalities, nonprofits, businesses, and their employees. He noted that air transport has become increasingly critical for rural communities, and the organization has expanded its local fleet from one helicopter a decade ago to three brand-new aircraft this year. Crocker explained that membership is not insurance; rather, it is a benefit offered directly by Air Medical Care Network, which owns both the aircraft and the crews. The program may be funded by the locality or offered as a voluntary payroll-deduct benefit to employees. Membership ensures that employees and all members of their household would not incur any out-of-pocket expenses if transported by one of the network’s aircraft, locally or nationwide. He emphasized the affordability of the program, which costs $70 per year, and described it as a proactive measure providing financial peace of mind in the event of an emergency air transport. Crocker closed by noting that preliminary discussions had taken place with city staff and that the program could be rolled out easily if the city chooses to proceed. Mrs. Foster asked if we currently needed to use a medivac, would we just go through insurance? Mr. Crocker responded that insurance will still be involved, but anything they did not cover, this program would with no out of pocket money. Mr. Wohlford asked Mr. Crocker if he knew how it worked if Medicare is involved. Mr. Crocker responded that it was his understanding that if you have Medicare B, you'll probably have somewhere between $1,500 and $2,000 out of pocket, but would get more information for him Mr. Gillespie said it was a good opportunity for the employees. Council agreed and requested a contract for their consideration PROCLAMATIONS: SUBJECT: Patriot Day SUMMARY: Patriot Day, is a holiday observed in the United States on September 11 to commemorate the lives of those who died in the 2001 terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Virginia and those who perished when the hijacked United Airlines Flight 93 crashed in Pennsylvania. The proclamation recognizes the significance of this event and the lives lost. ACTION: Mayor Horton made a motion to adopt the proclamation; Mrs. Artrip seconded the motion. VOTE: AYES: Mrs. Artrip, Mrs. Foster, Mr. Gillespie, Mr. Wohlford, Mayor Horton SUBJECT: Tribute to Heroes SUMMARY: The Radford Noon Rotary in collaboration with the Radford Heritage Foundation have had the “Tribute to Heroes” flags on display since Memorial Day to honor those heroes who have demonstrated extraordinary commitment, compassion and resilience. The closing ceremony was held on September 11, 2026. ACTION: Mrs. Foster made a motion to adopt the proclamation; Mr. Gillespie seconded the motion. VOTE: AYES: Mrs. Artrip, Mrs. Foster, Mr. Gillespie, Mr. Wohlford, Mayor Horton SUBJECT: Constitution Week SUMMARY: The week of September 17-23, 2026, is nationally recognized as “Constitution Week”. The Daughters of the American Revolution set aside the week to formally commemorate the importance of the document as a testament to liberty, freedom and inalienable rights. ACTION: Mayor Horton made a motion to adopt the proclamation; Mr. Artrip seconded the motion. VOTE: AYES: Mrs. Artrip, Mrs. Foster, Mr. Gillespie, Mr. Wohlford, Mayor Horton PUBLIC HEARINGS SUBJECT: School Board Budget Amendment
