title: Action Agenda
text: City of Roanoke, Virginia CITY COUNCIL September 21, 2026 2:00 PM City Council Chamber 215 Church Avenue, SW AGENDA The City of Roanoke is a safe, caring and economically vibrant community in which to live, learn, work, play and prosper. A vibrant urban center with strong neighborhoods set amongst the spectacular beauty of Virginia's Blue Ridge. NOTICE: Today's City Council meetings will be televised live and replayed on RVTV Channel 3 on Thursdays at 7:00 pm, and Saturdays from 10:00 am to 5:00 pm; and video streamed through YouTube Live at youtube.com/RoanokeVa. Council meetings are offered with closed captioning for the deaf or hard of hearing. 1. CALL TO ORDER - ROLL CALL. All present. A moment of silence was called by Mayor Joseph L. Cobb. The Pledge of Allegiance to the Flag of the United States of America was led by Mayor Cobb. Welcome ANNOUNCEMENTS: 2. PRESENTATIONS AND ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS: None. 3. HEARING OF CITIZENS UPON PUBLIC MATTERS: The City Council sets this time as a priority for citizens to be heard. All matters will be referred to the City Manager for response, recommendation or report to the Council, as she may deem appropriate. Grayson Coates, appeared before Council and spoke regarding blanket eviction bans for individuals with prior evictions or judgments. Danny Clawson, appeared before Council in support of collective bargaining for the Roanoke Firefighters Association. Duane Howard, appeared before Council and thanked Mayor Cobb for touring southeast with him. Mr. Howard requested assistance in addressing homeless encampments and abandoned vehicles in the area. He stated that the police are not enforcing violations. Chris Craft, appeared before Council and expressed opposition to data centers, the purchase of the Old Monterey Golf Course, and the proposed LD Cyrus Builders Inc. apartment development. Sylvia King, appeared before Council and thanked Council for working with Walmart to construct bus shelters at the Valley View location. She also raised concerns about Route 15 and its distance from Walmart, stating that the walk is difficult, especially during inclement weather. Christopher Tyler Breeding, appeared before Council and asked that the street design guidelines be updated to reflect current national standards on a defined timeline, including protected bike lane designs and the All Ages and Abilities standard. Eric Michael, appeared before Council and requested a referendum on automated license plate readers to allow voters to decide whether the technology should be used. 4. CONSENT AGENDA: APPROVED (7-0), AS AMENDED C-1. A communication from Mayor Joseph L. Cobb requesting that City Council convene in a Closed Meeting to discuss the Council's Code of Conduct and Ethics, pursuant to Section 2.2-3711 (A)(1), Code of Virginia (1950), as amended. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Concurred in the request. C-2. A communication from the City Attorney requesting that City Council convene in a closed meeting to consult with legal counsel requiring the provision of legal advice by the City Attorney regarding the City's rights, obligations, and risks under applicable Virginia statutes governing employee relations, pursuant to Section 2.2-3711(A)(8), Code of Virginia (1950), as amended. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Concurred in the request. C-3. A communication from the City Attorney requesting that City Council convene in a closed meeting to consult with legal counsel employed or retained by a public body regarding specific legal matters requiring the provision of legal advice by such counsel concerning the disposition of City real property in the Northwest part of the City, pursuant to Section 2.2-3711 (A)(8), Code of Virginia, (1950), as amended. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Concurred in the request. C-4. A communication from the City Manager requesting that City Council convene in a closed meeting for the purpose of discussing possible disposition of property in the Northwest part of the City, where discussion in an open meeting would adversely affect the bargaining position or negotiating strategy of the public body, pursuant to Section 2.2-3711 (A)(3), Code of Virginia, (1950), as amended. Withdrawn RECOMMENDED ACTION: Concur in the request. C-5. A communication from the City Manager requesting that City Council convene in a closed meeting for the purpose of discussing possible disposition of property in the Southwest part of the City, where discussion in an open meeting would adversely affect the bargaining position or negotiating strategy of the public body, pursuant to Section 2.2-3711 (A)(3), Code of Virginia, (1950), as amended. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Concurred in the request. C-6. A communication from the City Clerk advising of the resignation of Byron L. Hamlar as a member of the Board of Zoning Appeals, effective immediately. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Accepted the resignation and received and filed the communication. C-7. Reports of qualification of Kenneth Wilkerson as a member of the Towing Advisory Board for a three-year term of office, commencing November 1, 2026, and ending October 31, 2029; and Brittney Flowers as a member of the Equity and Empowerment Advisory Board to replace Danielle Johnson for a term of office ending December 31, 2026. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Received and filed. At 2:29 p.m., the Council Meeting was declared in recess for a Closed Meeting; and thereafter reconvened at 3:28 p.m. REGULAR AGENDA: 5. PUBLIC HEARINGS: None. 6. PETITIONS AND COMMUNICATIONS: 7. 1. Presentation of the Roanoke Firefighters Association to share information on collective bargaining. Todd Reighley, President, Spokesperson. (Sponsored by Council Members Sanchez-Jones and Nash) Received and filed. 2. Appropriation of funds as reimbursement to the City Treasurer as a Licensed Agency of the Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) - DMV Select Program. Adopted Ordinance No. 43468-092126. (7-0) REPORTS OF CITY OFFICERS AND THE CITY MANAGER: 1. City Manager: BRIEFINGS: None. ITEMS RECOMMENDED FOR ACTION: a. Acceptance and Appropriation of the Roanoke FY26 Safer Communities Program Grant. Adopted Ordinance No. 43469-092126. (7-0) b. Acceptance and Appropriation for the 2027 Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles for highway safety grant - Alcohol. Adopted Ordinance No. 43470-092126. (7-0) c. Acceptance and Appropriation for the 2027 Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles for highway safety grant - Police Traffic Services. Adopted Ordinance No. 43471-092126. (7-0) d. Acceptance and Appropriation of the 2025 BJA FY25 Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant Program. Adopted Ordinance No. 43472-092126. (7-0) COMMENTS OF THE CITY MANAGER. The City Manager offered the following comments: Gilmer Traffic Calming Project Staff recently joined community volunteers and local artists for the Gilmer Traffic Calming Project, preparing five sites and completing the first of five planned street murals. The first mural honors the Star City Medical Society and the legacy of Black medical professionals who served Roanoke during the Jim Crow era, and the project has already brought residents together to talk about both the history and future of Gilmer Avenue. Pickleball Signs Our Park Maintenance staff have completed the installation of pickleball signs and equipment boxes at four neighborhood parks—Shrine Hill, Belmont, Raleigh Court, and Eureka. Beginning September 15, players at these locations are required to use quieter pickleballs, and the City is providing those balls at the courts to help players make the transition while keeping the courts enjoyable for nearby residents. Employee Passing I also want to take a moment to recognize the unexpected passing of a valued member of our Parks and Recreation team. Anthony Caudle was a highly experienced member of our Urban Forestry staff who brought tremendous knowledge, professionalism, and expertise to his work caring for Roanoke’s urban forest, and he will be deeply missed by his colleagues and the many people he served. PUBLIC MATTERS FOLLOW-UP Carol Corbin, Communications Manager, reported on the following matters from the August 17 and September 8 meetings: Greenway Connectivity in NW and the Safety Action Plan At the August 17 meeting, one resident spoke regarding greenway connectivity in northwest and the Safety Action Plan. They were connected with the City’s Safe Streets for All and Vision Zero Coordinator who worked to provide them with safer, alternative routes that are primarily on 25 mph neighborhood roads and greenways. The resident was also connected with the Loudon-Melrose Neighborhood Association for continued engagement. RPD Follow-up The Roanoke Police Department followed up with three residents who spoke on separate matters at the August 17 meeting. One resident spoke about trespassing and misconduct happening on their property on Elm Avenue. RPD has reached out to have the property enrolled in the Trespass Bar Program and Code Enforcement has cited the owner of an adjacent lot. As a result, the lot has been mowed and cleaned up resulting in less gathering and loitering. The Police Department will continue to monitor this area and address any future issues as needed. Another resident expressed concern about encampments in the area of 14th Street SE. In collaboration with Code Enforcement, the campsites located on this property were placed on notice to be vacated and the property owner was notified. As of Friday, September 18, the property was vacated and a crew was cleaning the area. The Police Department will continue to work within the applicable City Code to address and clean up these campsites. A third resident expressed concern about the operation of a food truck. RPD reports that the food truck owner has the proper permits to operate within the City. The Police Department found no legally enforceable violations related to this complaint. Wilmont Park Area Curbing At the September 8 meeting, a resident inquired about action on a longstanding request for curbing and stormwater runoff issues. The Engineering division reports that this project’s priority listing was #214 in 2000 and it is currently listed as #198. The City Stormwater team evaluated the property and discussed the runoff concern with the resident. They discovered that the water runoff the resident is experiencing results from the grade of the driveway on the property. Curb and gutter installation would not fix the runoff problem; it would only be aesthetic. Stormwater offered the property owner options for addressing the driveway water runoff. 2. CITY ATTORNEY: a. 3. 8. Adoption of an Ordinance amending and reordaining Section 2-316, Youth athletics review board, Article XIV, Authorities, boards, commissions and committees generally, Chapter 2, Administration, Code of the City of Roanoke (1979) as amended. Adopted Ordinance No. 43473-092126. (6-1, Vice-Mayor McGuire voted no.) DIRECTOR OF REAL ESTATE VALUATION: None. REPORTS OF COMMITTEES: 1. Comments on certain Authorities, Boards, Committees and Commissions in which City Council serve as liaisons or appointees. None. 9. UNFINISHED BUSINESS: None. 10. INTRODUCTION AND CONSIDERATION OF ORDINANCES AND RESOLUTIONS: 1. 11. 12. Repeal and replace Ordinance No. 43413-061526 approving and authorizing transfer of funds to local non-profit agencies recommended by the Human Services Advisory Board to correct an appropriation error. Adopted Ordinance No. 43474-092126. (7-0) MOTIONS AND MISCELLANEOUS BUSINESS: 1. Inquiries and/or comments by the Mayor and Members of City Council. None. 2. Vacancies on certain authorities, boards, commissions and committees appointed by Council. None. RECESSED - 4:29 p.m. The City Council Meeting will stand in recess; and thereafter reconvene at 7:00 pm, in the City Council Chamber, Room 450, Noel C. Taylor Municipal Building. City of Roanoke, Virginia CITY COUNCIL 7:00 pm City Council Chamber 215 Church Avenue, SW 13. CALL TO ORDER - ROLL CALL. All present. The Invocation was delivered by The Reverend Jen Raffensperger, Pastor, Unitarian Universalist Church of Roanoke. The Pledge of Allegiance to the Flag of the United States of America was led by Mayor Joseph L. Cobb. Welcome Certification of Closed Meeting. (7-0) 14. NEW BUSINESS: 1. 15. Adopted Resolution No. 43475-092126, creating a temporary ad hoc Professional Standards Committee. (6-1, Vice-Mayor McGuire voted no.) PRESENTATIONS AND ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS: Proclamation declaring the week of September 17–23, 2026, as Constitution Week. Mayor Cobb presented the proclamation to representatives of the Daughters of the American Revolution. Proclamation declaring the week of September 17 - 23, 2026 as Fishburn Legacy Week. Mayor Cobb presented the proclamation to representatives of Friends of Mountain View and the Fishburn family. Community Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Emissions and Energy Report and City Emissions Report - 30 minutes Received and filed. 16. PUBLIC HEARINGS: 1. Request of LD Cyrus Builders Inc., to rezone the property located at 2717, 2719 and three parcels addressed as 0 Colonial Avenue SW; bearing Official Tax Map Nos. 1260313, 1260808, 1260807, 1260806, and 1260805, respectively, from MX, Mixed Use District and R-7, Residential District to RMF, Residential District with conditions and CN, Commercial Neighborhood with conditions. Daniel Cyrus, Agent, Spokesperson. Adopted Ordinance No. 43476-092126. (6-0, Council Member Hagen was not present when the vote was recorded.) 2. 17. Receive citizen comments, prior to Council taking action to authorize General Obligation Bonds, a reimbursement request resolution and bond action timeline for the Fiscal Year 2026-2027 Capital Improvement Plan projects as endorsed as part of the annual Fiscal Year 2026-2027 budget adoption. Adopted Ordinance No. 43477-092126. (7-0) HEARING OF CITIZENS UPON PUBLIC MATTERS: The City Council sets this time as a priority for citizens to be heard. If deemed appropriate, matters will be referred to the City Manager for response, recommendation or report to the City Council. Kathleen Wooley, appeared before Council and spoke in support of collective bargaining for City employees. Brittany Deaton, appeared before Council and spoke in opposition to data centers. Jonathan Gros, appeared before Council and spoke in opposition to data centers. Michelle Derrico, appeared before Council and spoke in support of environmental stewardship of Wood Haven Park. Michelle Brooks, appeared before Council and spoke in support of collective bargaining for the Roanoke Firefighters Association. Clayton Ahuero, appeared before Council and spoke in support of collective bargaining for City employees. Owen McGuire, appeared before Council requesting that the remaining 15 acres of Fishburn Park land be designated as parkland and protected from development, and that the previously sold parcel and cottage be repurchased and restored as parkland. Megan Lisle, appeared before Council and spoke in support of collective bargaining for the Roanoke Firefighters Association and opposition to data centers. Dr. Brenda Hale, appeared before Council and spoke about concerns over the conduct and disparaging comments made by Vice-Mayor McGuire toward the City Manager. Emperial Young, appeared before Council and spoke in opposition to data centers. August Arzaga, appeared before Council and spoke in opposition to data centers. Danny Clawson, appeared before Council spoke about substance abuse disorders among first responders and opposition to data centers. Mark Burton, appeared before Council and asked questions regarding the greenhouse gas emissions report, while requesting a reconciliation of how the revenues from the one percent meals tax have been spent, including completed projects and the amount of funds spent on each project. Ben Verschoor, appeared before Council and spoke in opposition to data centers. Jeff Leff, appeared before Council in support of collective bargaining for the Roanoke Firefighters Association and opposition to data centers. Dominic Harden, appeared before Council in support of collective bargaining for the Roanoke Firefighters Association and opposition to data centers. Joy Truskowski, appeared before Council in support of collective bargaining for the Roanoke Firefighters Association and opposition to data centers. Willard Simpson, appeared before Council in support of collective bargaining for the Roanoke Firefighters Association. ADJOURNED - 9:25 p.m.

BY-LAWS Of the CUMBERLAND COUNTY, VIRGINIA PLANNING COMMISSION Adopted: January 12, 2026 ARTICLE I – AUTHORIZATION 1.1. 1.2. This Planning Commission is re-established in conformance with action by the Board of Supervisors of Cumberland, Virginia, on September 1, 1989, and in accord with the provisions of Section 15.2-2210, Code of Virginia (1950), as amended. The official title of this body shall be the Cumberland County Planning Commission, hereinafter referred to as the “Commission.” ARTICLE II – PURPOSE 2.1. The primary purpose of the Commission is to serve in an advisory capacity to the Board of Supervisors by preparing and recommending plans, ordinances, capital 5 PC Minutes 20260112 Page 2 of 12 improvements program, and other documents to the Board of Supervisors for its consideration. ARTICLE III – MEMBERSHIP 3.1. The Commission shall consist of seven (7) voting members appointed by the Board of Supervisors. All shall be residents of Cumberland County and qualified by knowledge and experience to make decisions on questions of growth and development. At least half of the members shall own real property in Cumberland County. In addition to the seven (7) voting members, the Board of Supervisors may appoint one of its members to serve on the Commission as an ex officio member. 3.2. The terms of office for the Board of Supervisors member and the county planner and/or zoning administrator shall be coextensive with their terms of office, or until the Board of Supervisors appoints their replacement. The term of the members shall be for three (3) years. Subsequent members shall be appointed for terms of three (3) years. The Board of Supervisors, at its discretion, may establish different terms of office for initial and subsequent appointments, including terms of office concurrent with those of the Board of Supervisors. 3.3. Vacancies shall be filled by appointment made by the Board of Supervisors and shall be for an unexpired term only. 3.4. Members of the Commission shall be eligible for reappointment. 3.5. Planning Commission members shall be encouraged to attend a certified planning commission course within six (6) months of the member’s initial appointment. 3.6. Members of the Commission shall attempt to attend all meetings and shall not be absent from more than one-third of the total Commission meetings during any calendar year without just cause. A letter from the Secretary to the member shall be sent after any member is absent for more than one-third of the total Commission meetings during any calendar year or is absent from three consecutive regular meetings. Any such letter shall provide the member with a warning that further absences may be deemed to constitute malfeasance in office and may result in his or her removal from the Planning Commission by the Board of Supervisors. 3.7. In addition to the reasons set forth in Sec. 3.6, members may be removed by the Board of Supervisors for any other acts of malfeasance in office. 3.8. Terms of the Commission members shall expire immediately before the beginning of the regular meeting, at which time their successors’ terms of office begin. 3.9. Members of the Planning Commission shall be compensated according to the amount set by the Board of Supervisors. 6 PC Minutes 20260112 Page 3 of 12 ARTICLE IV – SELECTION OF OFFICERS 4.1. Officers of the Commission shall consist of a chairman, vice-chairman and secretary. The chairman and the vice-chairman shall be elected by the membership. The county planner and/or zoning administrator will be appointed to serve as the secretary to the Planning Commission without voting privileges. 4.2. Nomination of officers shall be made from the floor at the January meeting each year. Election of officers shall follow immediately. A candidate receiving a majority vote of the membership present and voting shall be declared elected. 4.3. Vacancies shall be filled for an unexpired term by a majority vote of the Commission. ARTICLE V – DUTIES OF OFFICERS 5.1 The chairman shall: 5.1.1. 5.1.2. 5.1.3. 5.1.4. 5.1.5. 5.1.6. 5.1.7. 5.2 The vice-chairman shall: 5.2.1. 5.2.2. 5.3 Preside at meetings of the Planning Commission. Appoint committees. Rule on procedural questions (subject to reversal by a two-thirds vote of the members present). Report official communications at the next regular Commission meeting. Certify official documents involving the authority of the Commission. Certify minutes as true and correct copies. Carry out other duties as assigned by the Commission. Assume the full powers of the chairman in the absence of inability of the chairman to act. Carry out other duties as assigned by the Commission. The secretary shall: 5.3.1. 5.3.2. 5.3.3. 5.3.4. 5.3.5. 5.3.6. 5.3.7. Notify members of all meetings. Give notice and be responsible for publishing public notices of all Commission public hearings and public meetings. Attend to the correspondence necessary for the execution of the duties and functions of the Commission. Record attendance at all meetings. Record the minutes of the Commission meetings. Maintain a file of all official Commission records and reports. Certify maps, records, and reports of the Commission. 7 PC Minutes 20260112 Page 4 of 12 5.3.8. Carry out other duties as assigned by the Commission. ARTICLE VI – COMMITTEES 6.1 The following committees may be appointed at the discretion of the chairman. 6.1.1. Comprehensive Plan Committee – develops, updates, and revises the comprehensive plan and coordinates the work of other committees that are related to the plan development. 6.1.2. 6.1.3. 6.1.4. 6.2 Ordinance Committee – at the request of the Board of Supervisors, studies, reviews, and makes recommendations on issues affecting the County. Zoning and Mapping Committee – drafts zoning ordinance and subsequent amendments. Reviews applications for rezoning, special exceptions, or conditional use permits and makes recommendations to the Commission. Prepares and maintains an inventory of land uses within Cumberland County and is responsible for the preparation of land use maps. Draft subdivision regulations and subsequent amendments. Examines subdivision applications and makes recommendations to the Commission after reviewing staff comments. Capital Improvements Committee – prepares and annually updates a capital improvements program (CIP) in conjunction with Cumberland County administrative officials. Assures that the CIP is in conformance with the comprehensive plan. Special Committees may be appointed by the chairman for purposes and terms approved by the Commission. 6.2.1. 6.2.2. 6.2.3. 6.2.4. Committee meetings shall follow the same protocol as a regular meeting. Citizen input shall be allowed in all committee meetings but shall not exceed the time limit set by the committee chairman. Citizens can be appointed to subcommittees to work on special projects by the Planning Commission members serving on various committees. The subcommittee shall act in an advisory capacity to the committee that selected them. At least one Planning Commission member shall serve on the subcommittee. Citizens do not vote with the committee on an issue to go before the Planning Commission. ARTICLE VII – MEETINGS 8 PC Minutes 20260112 Page 5 of 12 7.1. Regular meeting dates and times of the Commission shall be established for the coming year at the Commission’s first meeting held in January. Special meetings shall be called as needed. When a meeting date falls on a legal holiday, the meeting shall be held on the day following, unless the Commission selects an alternate day. 7.2. Special meetings may be called by the chairman or by two members upon written request to the secretary. The secretary shall notify the members by electronic mail or by phone, at least five days before a special meeting, stating the time, place, and purpose of the meeting. 7.3. All meetings of the Commission shall be open to the public. 7.4. Individuals of the public desiring to speak during the general public comment period must first provide their identifying information on a signup sheet. Only residents of Cumberland County or individuals owning real property in Cumberland County are permitted to speak during the general public comment period. ARTICLE VIII – VOTING 8.1. A majority of the members shall constitute a quorum. 8.2. No action of the Commission shall be valid unless authorized by a majority vote of those present and voting. 8.3. Members from the Board of Supervisors and the administrative branch shall serve as non-voting members. 8.4. Chairman shall vote on all matters before the Commission as appropriate. ARTICLE IX – ORDER OF BUSINESS 9.1 The order of business for a regular meeting shall be: 9.1.1 9.1.2 9.1.3 9.1.4 9.1.5 9.1.6 9.1.7 9.1.8 9.1.9 9.1.10 9.1.11 9.1.12 Call to order Recording of roll Determination of a quorum Approval of Agenda Presentation of the invited speaker Approval of minutes Requests to set Public Hearings Public Hearings (when necessary) Report of standing committees Report of special committees Old business New business 9 PC Minutes 20260112 Page 6 of 12 9.1.13 9.1.14 9.1.15 General public comment (items not pertaining to a public hearing matter, up to, but not more than three minutes per person, and a maximum of thirty minutes total. This timeframe can be extended an additional 30 minutes at the discretion of the Chairman.) Announcements and remarks by the commissioners Adjournment The failure to adhere to the foregoing order of business shall not invalidate an action or recommendation of the Planning Commission. 9.2 The latest edition of Robert’s Rules of Order shall be used as a guideline to govern the parliamentary procedure of Commission meetings; provided, however, the failure to adhere to the parliamentary procedure set forth in Robert’s Rules of Order shall not invalidate an otherwise valid action or recommendation of the Planning Commission. 9.3 The Commission shall keep minutes of each meeting, and after approval, these minutes shall become a public record. The secretary and the chairman shall sign all minutes. ARTICLE X – PUBLIC HEARINGS 10.1. In addition to those required by law, the Commission may hold public hearings on any matter which it deems to be in the public interest. 10.2. Notice of a public hearing shall follow § 15.2-2204 of the Code of Virginia. 10.3. Individuals of the public wishing to speak during a public hearing must first provide their identifying information on a signup sheet. Only residents of Cumberland County or individuals owning real property in Cumberland County are permitted to speak at any public hearing. 10.4. The chairman shall summarize the matter before the Commission, allow technical presentations by qualified persons or firms, and allow interested citizens to speak. Time allowance will be at the discretion of the chairman. The chairman will accept written statements and other documentation pertinent to the matter being addressed; however, the chairman may recognize someone who has arrived late. 10.5. An accurate, written record shall be made of the proceedings of a public hearing, approved by the Commission and maintained as part of the Commission files. ARTICLE XI – AMENDMENTS 11.1. These By-Laws may be amended by a majority vote of the entire membership after seven (7) days prior to notice. 10 PC Minutes 20260112 Page 7 of 12 2026 PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING SCHEDULE MOTION: On a motion by Commissioner Allen, and seconded by Commissioner Flippen, the 2026 Planning Commission Meeting Schedule was adopted as presented. The motion passed 4-0. Items not removed may be adopted by general consent without debate. Attachments: Meeting Minutes Summary of Accounts Payable Recommendations: Staff recommends approval of items of consent. Possible Board Action(s): MOTION to APPROVE: I make a motion to approve the items of consent. 4 HENRY COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS MINUTES August 25, 2026 – 3:00 p.m. The Henry County Board of Supervisors held its regular meeting on August 25, 2026, at 3:00 p.m. in the Summerlin Meeting Room of the County Administration Building, 3300 Kings Mountain Road, Collinsville, Virginia. The following Board members were present: Jim Adams, Chairman; Travis Pruitt, Vice Chairman; Chris Lawless; Debra Buchanan; Garrett Dillard; and Pam Cobler. Staff members present were Dale Wagoner, County Administrator; JR Powell, Deputy County Administrator; George Lyle, County Attorney; Darrell Jones, Chief Financial Officer; Crystal Ferguson, Deputy Director of Finance; Michelle Via, Director of Human Resources; Brandon Martin, Public Information Officer; and Jennifer Gregory, Executive Assistant. Lt. Colonel Eric Hairston, Major Danny Harold, Captain Sandy Hines, and Sgt. Tim Robertson of the Sheriff's Office were present. Bill Wyatt of the Martinsville Bulletin, Taylor Boyd of the Henry County Enterprise, Charles Roark of Star News, and WSET ABC 13 were also present. INVOCATION AND PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE: Chairman Adams gave the invocation, and Mr. Lawless led the Pledge of Allegiance. CALL TO ORDER: Chairman Adams called the meeting to order and welcomed everyone. He stated that anyone wishing to be on the agenda for the Board's regular business meeting at 3:00 p.m. must contact the County Administrator's Office at least 7 days before the meeting. Those wishing to speak at the Board's public meeting starting at 6:00 p.m. may do so under the agenda item - Matters Presented by the Public, without contacting the County Administrator's Office. ITEMS OF CONSENT: Confirmation of Minutes of Meetings Copy included in Board's File.  July 28, 2026 (Regular Meeting) 5 Summary of Accounts Payable Copy included in Board's File.  August 25, 2026 Resolution Honoring the 80th Anniversary of the Fieldale Volunteer Fire Department Copy included in Board's File. Mr. Pruitt made a motion to approve the Items of Consent, and Ms. Buchanan seconded it. The motion was approved by the following vote: AYES: Adams, Buchanan, Cobler, Dillard, Lawless, and Pruitt. NAYS: None. MONTHLY REPORT ON DELINQUENT TAX COLLECTION EFFORTS Tiffanie S. Hairston, Treasurer, noted that 95.45% of 2025 real estate taxes and 89.82% of 2025 personal property taxes had been collected. Since January 1, 2026, TACS has collected approximately $828,011.17. In addition, TACS collected 453 Vehicle Registration Withholding (VRW) stops in June 2026 and 557 in July 2026. UPDATE FROM PIEDMONT COMMUNITY SERVICES Greg Preston, Executive Director of Piedmont Community Services (PCS), updated the Board on PCS matters (Copy included in Board’s File). UPDATE FROM BLUE RIDGE REGIONAL LIBRARY Melissa Chapman, Director of the Blue Ridge Regional Library, updated the Board on matters related to the regional library (Copy included in Board’s File). UPDATE FROM THE WEST PIEDMONT HIGHER EDUCATION CENTER Eric Jones, Chairman of the Board of Directors for the West Piedmont Higher Education Center, updated the Board on matters related to the center (Copy included in Board’s File). ADDITIONAL APPROPRIATION RE: RETURN TO LOCALITIES FUNDS – PUBLIC SAFETY Dale Wagoner, County Administrator, said Public Safety Director Tim Duffer is asking the Board to appropriate $54,672 received from the Virginia Department of Health’s Return to Locality Funds. The Return to Locality funds are derived from a fee for 6 each vehicle registered in Henry County. Authorized expenditures of the funds are for items such as emergency medical services training, supplies, and/or equipment. Mr. Duffer has stated that the funds will be used to purchase standardized medical supplies and to maintain the EMS pharmacy for all EMS agencies. This centralized purchasing model will ensure EMS agencies have access to authorized supplies and will support the operational readiness of the countywide EMS system. On a motion by Mr. Pruitt and seconded by Dr. Cobler, the Board approved the additional appropriation of $54,672 received from the Return to Localities Funds with the condition of further procedural development and approval by the Emergency Services Advisory Council by the following vote: AYES: Adams, Buchanan, Cobler, Dillard, Lawless, and Pruitt. NAYS: None. ADDITIONAL APPROPRIATION RE: VIRGINIA DEPARTMENT OF CRIMINAL JUSTICE SERVICES GRANT – SHERIFF’S OFFICE Dale Wagoner, County Administrator, said Sheriff Wayne Davis is asking the Board to approve an additional appropriation of $15,958 received from the Virginia Department of Criminal Justice Services (DCJS) through its Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant (JAG) program. Sheriff Davis stated the funds will cover overtime pay for highimpact law enforcement activities in areas experiencing an increase in crime. The grant does not require a local match. On a motion by Ms. Buchanan and seconded by Mr. Dillard, the Board approved the additional appropriation of $15,958 received from the DCJS grant as presented by the following vote: AYES: Adams, Buchanan, Cobler, Dillard, Lawless, and Pruitt. NAYS: None. PROPOSED ZONING ORDINANCE RE: DATA CENTERS George Lyle, County Attorney, said at the July 28, 2026, meeting of the Board of Supervisors, following a public hearing on proposed zoning amendments, the Board directed staff to research and develop a county ordinance for the zoning of data centers. County Attorney George Lyle presented an ordinance for the Board’s consideration: Article XX. – Data Center District D-C Sec. 21-2000. – Intent. The Data Center District is intended to allow for the regulation of data center developments that contribute to economic development and technological infrastructure, while ensuring compatibility with surrounding land uses. Development within this district shall be designed and operated to minimize adverse impacts on adjacent properties, public infrastructure, environmental resources, and the health, safety, and welfare of the community through design standards and mitigation measures. In addition to all regulations listed in Article XX, all development within the Data Center District shall also comply with Article XXI, Data Center Regulations. Sec. 21-2001. – Special use permit uses. The uses permitted in the Data Center District with a special use permit as approved by the Board of Zoning Appeals are as follows: 1. Data centers 10 Sec. 21-2002. – Area regulations. No minimum area regulations. Sec. 21-2003. – Setback regulations. The front setback line shall be located one hundred (100) feet from any street right-of-way. This shall be known as the “setback line.” No structure shall be constructed or placed closer to the front property line than the setback line. Sec. 21-2004. – Yard regulations. A. Side. The minimum side yard for all structures shall be one thousand (1,000) feet if the adjoining parcel is not zoned to an industrial classification, and five hundred (500) feet if the adjoining parcel is zoned to an industrial classification. B. Rear. The minimum rear yard for all structures shall be one thousand (1,000) feet if the adjoining parcel is not zoned to an industrial classification, and five hundred (500) feet if the adjoining parcel is zoned to an industrial classification. Sec. 21-2005. – Height regulations. Structures may be erected up to seventy-five (75) feet in height from grade. This requirement shall not apply to chimneys, water towers, monuments, parapet walls, flues, flagpoles, television antennae, radio aerials, and similar structures and necessary mechanical appurtenances. Towers and structures may be erected to a height greater than seventy-five (75) feet if a special use permit is approved by the Board of Zoning Appeals. Article XXI. – Data Center Regulations Sec. 21-2100. – Definitions. Clearly Audible Pure Tone. A sound that contains a distinct, continuous, or regularly recurring tone or pitch that is readily perceptible to a person with normal hearing and distinguishable from background sound. Examples include the humming, whining, buzzing, or droning commonly associated with transformers, cooling fans, compressors, pumps, or similar mechanical equipment. Data Center. A facility whose primary services are the storage, management, and processing of digital data and is used to house (i) computer and network systems, including associated components such as servers, network equipment and appliances, telecommunications, and data storage systems; (ii) systems for monitoring and managing infrastructure performance; (iii) equipment used for the transformation, transmission, distribution, or management of at least one 11 megawatt of capacity of electrical power and cooling, including substations, uninterruptible power supply systems, all electrical plant equipment, and associated air handlers; (iv) Internet-related equipment and services; (v) data communications connections; (vi) environmental controls; (vii) fire protection systems; and (viii) security systems and services Sec. 21-2101. – Applicability; permitting. A special use permit is required for each data center development proposed to be constructed, installed, or operated in Henry County. Sec. 21-2102.- Applications and procedures for data centers. In addition to the requirements of a Henry County special use permit, applications for a data center development shall include the following information: a) Project narrative. A narrative identifying the applicant, owner, and operator, and describing the proposed data center development, including an overview of the project and its location. b) Site plan. The site plan shall include the following information: i. Property lines, minimum required setback lines under this article, and any proposed setback lines that exceed the minimum requirements. ii. Existing and proposed buildings and structures, including preliminary location(s) of the proposed data center facility and its operational equipment. iii. Existing and proposed access roads, permanent entrances, temporary construction entrances, drives, turnout locations, and parking, including written confirmation from the Virginia Department of Transportation (“VDOT”) that all entrances satisfy applicable VDOT requirements. iv. All other requirements set out in section 21-110 and section 21-218. c) Water Supply Impact Study. Due to the potential for high-water demand, the applicant shall submit a water supply impact study prepared by a 3rd party. The consultant, who is to be approved by the County, shall show experience in public water supply planning, water resources engineering, or hydrogeologic investigations. No application for a data center shall be accepted as complete until the County determines that the water supply 12 impact study has been submitted and reviewed by staff. The County may retain, at the applicant’s expense, an independent consultant to review the study. The study shall include, at a minimum: i. Projected water demand (average day, peak day, peak hour). ii. Cooling technology description (evaporative, air-cooled, hybrid, etc.). iii. Building Auditorium, 414 N. Main Street MEETING #37 — August 27th At a Special Legislative meeting of the Board of Supervisors on Thursday, August 27th at 4:00 PM in the Admin. Building Auditorium: PRESENT: Carty Yowell, Chairman James Jewett, Vice-Chairman Jud Buchanan, Member Mike Snider, Member Nancy Sharman, Member Hannon Wright, County Attorney Jonathon Weakley, County Administrator Kimberly Turner, Deputy Clerk ABSENT: Brian Gordon, Deputy County Administrator SPECIAL GUEST: Reynolds Boadi, Office of Congressman Eugene Vindman (District Coordinator) Bryce Reeves, Virginia Senator Karen Hamilton, Virginia House of Delegates CALL TO ORDER, PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE & MOMENT OF SILENCE Chairman Yowell called the Board to order. The Pledge of Allegiance was recited, followed by a moment of silence. DETERMINE PRESENCE OF A QUORUM/ADOPTION OF AGENDA Chairman Yowell advised that a quorum was present. Vice-Chairman Jewett made a motion to adopt the agenda as presented, seconded by Supervisor Sharman. Aye: Yowell, Jewett, Buchanan, Snider, Sharman. Nay: (0) Abstain: (0) Absent: (0). OLD BUSINESS None. NEW BUSINESS 1. Legislative Priorities Presentations Chairman Yowell welcomed Senator Bryce Reeves and Delegate Karen Hamilton and thanked them for their service to Madison County and the Commonwealth. He noted that Reynolds Boadi, District Coordinator for Congressman Eugene Vindman's office, would also participate, but had not yet arrived. Return to Agenda The County Administrator explained that the County had convened the meeting early in the legislative planning cycle so local priorities could be presented before the next General Assembly session. Presenters were asked to summarize each issue and allow time for questions and discussion. a. Fiscal Impact Fees Mr. Jim Smith presented information concerning local fiscal impact fees and the reduced ability to address development costs through proffers outside the rezoning process. Mr. Smith explained that residential growth can increase education, health and welfare, public safety, and generalgovernment costs that are not fully offset by new revenue. The County requested enabling authority for localities to impose impact fees so growth-related infrastructure and service costs would not be shifted entirely to existing taxpayers. Mr. Smith noted support for the concept from VACo and the Virginia Chapter of the American Planning Association and thanked the legislators for supporting the prior session's legislation. b. Agritourism Vice-Chairman Jewett discussed concerns that some venue operators may rely on the agritourism provisions of the Virginia Code to avoid local zoning requirements governing short-term rentals. Vice-Chairman Jewett described situations in which a minimal agricultural connection was asserted as the basis for adding lodging units beyond local limits. The County requested clarification of state law so agritourism protections could not be used to circumvent otherwise applicable local zoning ordinances, while recognizing that any statutory language would need to be workable beyond Madison County. c. Community Paramedicine (Treat-in-Place) Ms. Tiffany Rannebarger, Captain of Community Paramedicine, presented the County's community paramedicine pilot program, which uses specially trained paramedics to provide preventive assistance in patients' homes, including medication review, fall-risk reduction, chronic-disease education, telehealth support, and connections to other services. She reported that a seven-patient cohort declined from 38 calls before enrollment to two calls after the intervention, a 94.7 percent reduction; approximately 24 transports and 86.5 ambulancereadiness hours were preserved, with an estimated financial and operational benefit of $31,491. She also reported 90 referrals, 44 resolved cases, 15 ongoing patients, and installations of fallalert devices and smoke alarms. The County requested support for federal treat-in-place reimbursement proposals and state Rural Health Transformation funding for community paramedicine. District Coordinator Boadi arrived during the community paramedicine presentation. d. Collective Bargaining The County Administrator addressed proposals that would require collective bargaining by local governments. He stated that Madison County periodically reviews employee pay and Return to Agenda classifications and must compete with larger neighboring jurisdictions, but emphasized that employment and compensation decisions should remain local because conditions differ among communities. He asked the legislators to oppose a statewide mandate and suggested that, if additional requirements advance, regional compensation studies could provide a more appropriate basis for local salary decisions. e. Commonwealth's Attorney The Commonwealth's Attorney, Clarissa Berry, requested statutory clarification to reduce duplicative protective orders issued from related charges and to ensure that criminal complaints and victim contact information from magistrates reach the prosecuting office promptly. She asked that federal Victims of Crime Act funding not be reduced and encouraged consideration of a more stable state funding mechanism for victim-witness programs. She also discussed the effect of limiting inpatient competency-restoration services for persons charged with misdemeanors, the disproportionate effect of statewide mandates on small prosecutors' offices, and the importance of preserving locally elected prosecutors' discretion. The County Attorney arrived during the Commonwealth's Attorney presentation. f. Commissioner of the Revenue The Commissioner of the Revenue, Brian Daniel, opposed proposed centralized state administration of the local transient occupancy tax. He stated that local staff already administer the tax, understand local businesses and jurisdictional boundaries, and can do so without creating an additional state administrative structure. He asked that transient occupancy tax administration remain with the localities. The County Administrator noted the tax's importance to tourism funding and the need to monitor changing lodging activity. g. Animal Control (Enhanced Benefits) The Chief Animal Control Officer, Greg Cave, requested amendment of the Virginia hazardousduty retirement provisions to include full-time animal control officers or authorize a local option for enhanced benefits. Citing a 2023 JLARC report, he described risks from aggressive animals, livestock, rabies and other zoonotic diseases, and reported that animal control has a comparatively high workers' compensation claim rate. He noted that animal control officers enforce state and local laws and that comparable public-safety positions rated at lower risk receive enhanced benefits. He stated that the change would support recruitment and retention. Senator Reeves asked how animal control officers are classified in other jurisdictions and stated that his staff would research the matter. h. Circuit Court The Clerk of the Circuit Court, Leeta Louk, requested restoration of the traditional two-thirds state and one-third local funding allocation, revision of population-based Compensation Board staffing and salary thresholds for clerks' offices, and adequate funding for deputy-clerk career Return to Agenda development. She explained that small offices perform the same statutory functions as larger offices with substantially fewer employees and that unfunded records-sealing requirements add significant workload. The County Administrator and Clerk also discussed fraud risks associated with electronic land-record filings. The Clerk supported continued use of Virginia Property Records Alert, urged caution regarding electronic filing of wills, and emphasized the continuing need for careful document review. Senator Reeves acknowledged the concerns surrounding electronic filing and property fraud and discussed the potential for technology, including artificial intelligence, to assist with document review. i. Building and Zoning The Building and Zoning Director, Jamie Wilks, asked that changes affecting construction permitting be made through Virginia's established building-code process. He explained that recently enacted residential solar permitting provisions placed responsibilities under a separate title of the Virginia Code, creating potential conflicts concerning plan review, permitting, inspection, and local systems. Delegate Hamilton stated that she had heard similar concerns and planned to pursue an amendment or repeal. The County Administrator stated that he would provide the legislative guests with the presenters’ contact information to facilitate any necessary follow-up. He also emphasized the importance of enforceable solar-decommissioning plans. j. Social Services Social Services staff, Lauren Gordon, presented priorities of the Virginia League of Social Services Executives. She opposed centralized child protective services intake because transferring local reports to a Richmond call center could delay responses and result in the loss of important knowledge about local residents and relationships. She urged replacement of the Virginia Case Management System, describing longstanding system errors, manual workarounds, benefit-processing delays, and heightened financial exposure associated with the statewide error rate. She also described severe workforce challenges, including ten employee departures during the preceding year, lengthy training requirements, and competition with neighboring deviating agencies that can offer higher compensation. District Coordinator Boadi asked what measures could help alleviate the case-management system’s burdens and ensure that the County did not miss available assistance. Ms. Gordon reiterated the need for a replacement system or additional state funding. Senator Reeves discussed the possible reasons for centralizing child protective services intake and offered to obtain additional information regarding the proposal. k. Tourism Tourism and Economic Development Director, Tracy Gardner, supported human-trafficking identification and prevention training for short-term-rental operators, opposed hospitality- Return to Agenda specific taxes not supported by local tourism partners, and requested continued Virginia Tourism Corporation and welcome-center funding. She also supported public fishing access and naturalresource stewardship, site-characterization funding, GO Virginia, and Small Business Development Centers. The County Administrator requested information concerning potential state funding for future water and wastewater infrastructure projects. Senator Reeves discussed available infrastructure funding and requested information regarding the condition, needs, and priorities of the County’s system to support further review. l. Madison County Public Schools Superintendent Anna Graham and School Board members Lauren Gordon and Graham Davidson presented school priorities. They requested implementation of the JLARC economies-of-scale recommendation for divisions with fewer than 2,000 students, which was estimated to provide approximately $1.7 million to Madison County, and explained the higher per-pupil cost of operating a comprehensive rural high school. They requested an extension of locally awarded teacher licenses beyond one year and continued funding for the Future Educators Academy grow-your-own lab-school program. The group then discussed the referendum-based local-option sales tax for school capital projects, projected long-term school facility needs exceeding $100 million, and estimated annual revenue of $1.3 million to $1.5 million. The County Administrator requested continued state support for school resource officer grants, noting an estimated local impact of approximately $78,000 if the funding were discontinued. He also requested assistance concerning the proposed retirement of copper telephone service in remote areas, particularly where 911, alarm, and medical-alert services could be affected. Senator Reeves discussed the challenges of securing state funding for rural school divisions and emphasized that revenue from the proposed local-option sales tax should remain restricted to school capital projects. District Coordinator Boadi asked whether the County had explored available federal grants and offered to assist with identifying potential funding opportunities. The County Administrator stated that the County would welcome assistance in identifying state and federal grants and other financing options. He explained that the School System was commissioning a feasibility study to evaluate renovation, replacement, or a combination of improvements for the middle and high school campus. He also explained that much of the County’s fund balance is maintained pursuant to established financial policies and expressed concern that funding programs may view those reserves as readily available when evaluating the County’s financial need. Source: Page County, VA 6 PAGE COUNTY HOUSING PLAN CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND Overview of Housing Study Overview of Housing Study The price of housing in Page County has skyrocketed over 46% since 2021. Because housing prices have grown faster than local wages have, entry-level and attainable housing has almost entirely disappeared from the local market. County residents often find it difficult to afford the available stock in Page and have been forced to find homes elsewhere. Major employers have had to put off planned expansion due to the lack of available housing for their workers. On top of this, some houses are purchased for conversion to short-term rentals. While it is a relatively small number – only about 7% of the houses sold during this period were so converted – it is a significant source of local concern and new developments must take this into consideration. Due to the high cost of construction, new, non-short-term-rental housing development has been difficult for the county to attract. cultural regions of the County and the more developed town centers. The Page County EDA’s site on Goodrich Road is in Stanley’s Secondary CSA. It has adequate infrastructure to handle moderate housing growth, and the location helps provide a buffer between rural, unincorporated areas of Page County and the dense Town of Stanley. As of 2026, approximately 23,548 people reside in Page County. The median household income in Page County is $65,980, which is somewhat below other median incomes in the region. Comparatively, the median household income in the Shenandoah Valley region is $80,732 and the median household income in the state of Virginia is $99,752. Page County’s housing stock is predominantly single-family, owner-occupied housing. Among occupied housing units in the County, 72% are owner-occupied and 28% are renter occupied. Local developers have claimed that it is hard to build houses in the area that can sell profitably under $300,000, but Page County residents often cannot afford more than $250,000. County residents across all ages and all over the economic spectrum feel pressure to move: young people cannot afford to enter the local housing market, and seniors cannot afford to downsize to a more appropriately sized home in the County. Affordability and conservation are key goals of this study. The Page County Comprehensive Plan prioritizes the development of attainable housing while retaining a rural and agricultural character. To aid in this goal, the County designated Community Service Areas (CSAs) to help target growth and limit sprawling development. CSAs are located around incorporated towns and along major corridors to help preserve the rural character and limit dense development in most unincorporated parts of the County, acting as a buffer between rural, agri- Approximately 50% of the local workforce commutes out of the County for work, and over 25% of residents commute over 60 minutes to work. People who live in Page County are there for other, mostly lifestyle reasons: family, the natural beauty, and an overall feeling of safety. Residents want to see development that they can afford and allows them to continue to have the quality and way of life that Page County has had for generations. This project seeks to identify local housing priorities and provide the County with a feasible housing development program that helps residents afford Page County. Stanley, Virginia. text: AGENDA Page County Planning Commission Work Session Board of Supervisors Room- County Government Center 103 South Court Street, Luray, VA 22835 September 22, 2026 - 7:00 p.m. Live Meeting Stream: http://www.pagecounty.virginia.gov/392/Watch-Meetings-Videos ___ Call to Order A. Pledge of Allegiance B. Moment of Silence C. Microphone Reminder D. Attendance Roll Call Adoption of Agenda New Business A. Adoption of Minutes: August 25, 2026 B. Flowerdew Hundred LLC- Special Use Permit Tracy Clatterbuck Unfinished Business A. Subdivision of Land Discussion Josh Hahn Adjourn MINUTES PAGE COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION August 25, 2026 Members Present Catherine Grech, Vice Chair, District 1 Jared Burner, Chairman, District 3 William Turner, District 5 Chris Adams, District 2 Sandy Davis, Secretary, District 4 Ken Johnson, At-Large Member Absent None Staff Present Josh Hahn Call to Order Chairman Burner called the August 25, 2026 Page County Planning Work Session to order in the Board of Supervisors (BOS) Room located at the Page County Government Center, 103 S Court Street, Luray, Virginia at 7:00 p.m. The call to order was followed by The Pledge of Allegiance and a Moment of Silence. Chairman Burner reminded all commissioners and speakers to please turn on and/or speak into the microphones. Mr. Hahn conducted an attendance roll call. Adoption of Agenda Chairman Burner explained staff had requested the agenda be amended to add EDA Housing Subcommittee Report after the Speedway under Unfinished Business. Mr. Johnson made a motion to adopt the agenda, as amended. Ms. Davis seconded the motion. The motion passed (6-0). New Business A. Adoption of Minutes: August 11, 2026 Chairman Burner allowed time to review the minutes. Mr. Tuner made a motion to adopt the minutes, as presented. Ms. Davis seconded the motion. Chairman Burner asked Mr. Hahn to conduct a roll call. The motion passed, unanimously (6-0). Unfinished Business A. Shenandoah Speedway Properties LC SUP Amendment (2007 Motor-Sport Park and 2011 Motocross Track – Dirt Track) Mr. Hahn referenced material in the packet, including an updated redline document, which Ms. Grech and Mr. Johnson worked on. He noted that there were many different colors in the document, which is a reflection of many different people updating the draft throughout the process. He noted an addendum to the packet, which was an email received from a citizen regarding the current draft, which may be referenced later. He noted a second addendum, which was his comments in response to the citizen comments regarding language in the Violations section of the conditions. Ms. Grech stated they spent collectively, many, many hours. She is aware that the results aren't going to please many people, but they really worked very hard on that. She thanked Mr. Johnson, Mr. Hahn, and Ms. Richards, who wasn’t present. She explained some of the thought Planning Commission Minutes- August 25, 2026 process. She has been on the Planning Commission about six, seven years now. This is by far the most difficult one, second to the SUP for industrial solar. This is really not easy. And had they had the benefit of professional advice or guidance, either through a sound study or just some conversation, it would have made it much easier. It has felt like the blind leading the blind. She was trying to keep as much of the old SUPs as possible, because she thought they were well thought out and reasoned, especially the 2007 permit, because they came in the wake of a sound study and recommendations by a professional. Number two, after keeping as much as they could, she thought they needed to clarify some definitions, some language, some metrics, where it was necessary to enable better enforcement where possible. They have heard that enforcement, for a variety of reasons, wasn't optimal, and some of it had to do with the way the rules were either not defined or not clearly – or the language needed modifications or maybe new metrics. Regarding enforcement, she knows there have been a lot of complaints from the public about lack of enforcement. That is not something that the Planning Commission, other than writing rules, has a direct influence on. That's something which is a budgetary item, and that is really a poor decision. They can write rules which they think that staff should be able to enforce, given the right tools or the personnel, but that's not a decision they can make at the level of the Planning Commission. They needed to modify definitions, language or metrics, and sometimes create some, when it was necessary to do so for public health and safety, trying to take into account the comments of the public, and also what Mr. Vaughan requested. That was the method. She provided a quick overview of the SUP, and which sections had been worked on. Discussion mainly included the following: • Ms. Grech and staff discussed different definitions added to clarify practices, public service use, and commercial use. There was lengthy discussion. Mr. Vaughan was invited to the front and there was further discussion. He indicated he was fine with the definitions. • There was a lack of consensus about having separate racing seasons for the oval track and the motocross track. Ms. Grech noted Mr. Hahn preferred to term the motocross track something different, as it is used for events other than motocross. Discussion on this was deferred to later. • There was lengthy discussion about having different decibel levels for practice, tuning, and testing, and no consensus was reached during that discussion about limiting practice, tuning and testing by decibel level or by number of times per week/year. Jeff Vaughan approached the podium. He stated, based on the progress that's been generated in the last hour, in the last months, he’d like to publicly pull the permit [and its] many amendments, and they'll operate as is. He thanked them for their time and the money they spent for the attorney fees. B. EDA Housing Subcommittee Report Ms. Davis summarized the subcommittee meeting from the previous day. It was meet and greet, and they talked about the Housing Study that's been completed. Some brainstorming occurred, but it was basically meeting each other and going over what they felt like were the challenges of affordable housing in the county and different grants. It was basically a strategic planning discussion. Mr. Hahn added that the public hearing for the short-term rentals, which will be at the Luray High School, will be the same night that the Housing Study is actually presented by the contractor to the Board. Chairman Burner adjourned the meeting at 8:02 p.m. ___ Jared Burner, Chairman Page 3 of 3 COUNTY OF PAGE 103 South Court Street, Suite F Luray, Virginia 22835 (540) 743-4142 Fax: (540) 743-4533 Board of Supervisors: Clifton ”Bucky” Thomas -Chairman -AtLarge Jeremy Baldwin -District 1 Allen Louderback - District 2 Ryan Cubbage -District 3 Susan Kile -District 4 Jeff Vaughan -District 5 County Administrator: Amity Moler TO: Page County Planning Commission FROM: Tracy Clatterbuck, Zoning Administrator I SUBJECT: Flowerdew Hundred LLC- Special Use Permit Application (Introduction) DATE: September 15, 2026 SUMMARY: Special use permit (SUP) to operate a self-storage facility. BACKGROUND: Flowerdew Hundred LLC has filed an application for a special use permit (SUP) to construct a self-storage facility located off US Hwy 340, Stanley, VA, and further identified by tax map number 59-(A)-63F. The parcel of land, currently vacant, is located west of Stanley, approximately 0.8 mile north of US HWY BSN 340 W and just to the north of 2845 US Hwy 340 Stanley. The property contains 9.69 acres and is currently zoned as Agriculture (A-1). The applicant is proposing to construct a self-storage facility for up to 500 self-serve storage units in a mix of the following sizes: 5x5, 5x10, 10x10, 10x15, 10x20, and 10x30. Under Section 125-4 of the Page County Zoning Ordinance, self-storage is defined as follows: SELF STORAGE: A structure or structures containing separate storage spaces of varying sizes leased or rented as individual leases for the purpose of storing personal property and household goods. In the A-1 zoning district, pursuant to Section 125-10.D(19) of the Page County Zoning Ordinance, self-storage units require a SUP. Also, the applicant will be required to comply with the following supplemental code regulations found under Section 125-30.19 (Self-Storage Facilities) of the Page County Zoning Ordinance: A. No commercial activities of any kind shall occur within the facility other than rental of storage units. No repair of vehicles, furniture, or other materials or equipment shall occur within the facility. Signs shall be posted within the facility describing such limitations. B. No storage of hazardous, toxic or explosive materials shall occur in the self-storage facility. Signs shall be posted within the facility describing such limitations. C. The maximum size of any individual storage space or unit in a self-storage facility shall be 500 square feet. D. In the Agriculture Zoning District, fencing, screening, and security may be required for all facilities. Additional conditions may also be required as part of the special use permit review process. E. Self-storage facilities shall not include portable storage containers, shipping containers and/or tractor trailers. The applicant has provided a detailed narrative explaining the proposal along with a concept plan and comp plan references. Draft conditions are included in the packet for review and consideration. They are merely a starting point for discussion with the Planning Commission. As indicated in the supplemental regulations listed above, additional conditions may also be considered relating to fencing, screening, and security. OTHER AGENCY COMMENTS: Virginia Department of Transportation (VDOT) – Per Lindsey Burgess with VDOT: 1) The location of the proposed commercial entrance meets VDOT requirements for sight distance. 2) Any access to a state-maintained roadway must be in accordance with Appendix F of the VDOT Road Design Manual. 3) At the site plan phase, VDOT will review and require the design of the new commercial entrance to meet all applicable state standards. 4) A VDOT land use permit will be required for any work within the VDOT right of way and may be obtained at the VDOT Harrisonburg residency office. Should the safety, use, or maintenance level of any existing or proposed entrance to a VDOT maintained highway change in the future, VDOT reserves the right to require additional modifications as warranted by the site-specific conditions. Staff recommends that we make requirements from VDOT a condition of the SUP. Health Department- Per Jeffery Mason with the Page County Health Department, “No health department issues w/ request. Note: Certification letters could be potentially Null/Void if drainfield areas are disturbed.” Staff recommends that we make requirements from the Health Department a condition of the SUP. Building Official- Per James Campbell, Page County Building Official, “No objection to request. Applicable permits will be required prior to construction.” Staff recommends that we make the requirements from the Building Official a condition of the SUP. PAGE COUNTY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: Tax Map 59-(A)-63F is located in the “Agricultural Protection Tier.” Per the Comprehensive Plan, the purpose of the Agricultural Protection Tier is “[t]o protect (to keep from being damaged or lost) agricultural uses and preserve the rural lifestyle and sense of community that has long defined Page County” (Volume 1-9). Further, the Comprehensive Plan states the following: “This tier is intended primarily for very low-density residential development, large lot rural development and agricultural uses. Non-residential uses would serve the needs of residents in the surrounding rural areas and generally be limited to agriculture-related businesses.” (Volume 1-23, 24). Policies within the Comprehensive Plan (Volume I, Chapter 3) include (other policies may also be relevant): • Goal 2, Policy 2.1: “Preserve a rural lifestyle in the County outside of the towns, Incorporated Areas Tier and Community Service Area Tiers.” (Volume 1-66). • Goal 3, Policy 3.2: “Preserve and protect agricultural uses and the rural lifestyle and sense of community that has long defined Page County, especially in the Agricultural Protection Tier.” (Volume 1-68). • Goal 3, Policy 3.16: “Minimize conflicts between agriculture and non-agricultural land uses. (Volume 1-70). • Goal 6, Policy 6.2: “Encourage economic growth that is compatible with the County's rural character while generating a positive net cash flow for the County” (Volume 1-74). • Goal 6, Policy 6.9: “Encourage commercial and industrial business to locate in industrial parks and existing commercial centers or designated growth areas” (Volume 1-74). • Goal 6, Policy 6.10: “Allow commercial and industrial uses in rural areas or near existing neighborhoods only if the use: a. Does not unduly impede traffic flow on roads or intersections; b. Is not, and does not, initiate strip development; c. Has direct access to adequate roads, railroads or airports; d. Meets all standards for water, sewage and waste disposal; and e. Does not adversely affect surrounding agricultural or residential activities” (Volume 1-74). Tax Map 59-(A)-63F is a portion of a larger lot that was divided via 25-acre divisions and non-family divisions, along with a boundary line adjustment, in 2024, as well as court-authorized divisions in 2025. The only residential address located within approximately 500 ft. of Tax Map 59-(A)-63F is 2844 US HWY 340, located on the west side of US HWY 340. 2845 US HWY 340 is the physical address for a poultry structure located approximately 50 ft. from the southwest parcel line of 59-(A)-63F. 2195 US HWY 340 is the address for structures previously operated as Page Valley Flea Market, located within a Commercial (C-1) split-zoned portion of Tax Map 59-(A)-40. This split-zoned portion of lot 59-A-40 is approximately 60 ft. from one corner of Tax Map 59-A-63F. Tax Map 59-(A)-63F does not have access to public water or wastewater. Contained within in the application packet is the applicant’s “Comprehensive Plan Compliance Narrative,” which includes a table of policies and consistency analysis of most of the policies listed, above. Planning staff generally concurs with the conclusions represented, here, including the assertion that the Zoning Ordinance reflects “the County’s own determination that a facility of this type can coexist with the district’s agricultural purpose without altering the land’s underlying agricultural zoning or availability for future agriculture use.” Staff notes that “rural character” may be interpreted in different ways. The Comprehensive Plan provides a general framework in Exhibit 5: Development Guidelines; however, a commercial storage land use does not necessarily fit cleanly within the “Rural Business” category. The Zoning Ordinance’s allowance of this use in the Agriculture zoning district by special use permit suggests that Rural Business may be a comparable “Land Use Type” from Exhibit 5. Staff recommends the Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors consider appropriate conditions to address potential adverse impact of this use brought forward during the public hearing(s). MOTION(S): I move that the Page County Planning Commission hold a public hearing on the SUP application for tax map number 59-(A)-63F at the Regular Meeting on October 13, 2026, and direct staff to provide adequate notice of such hearing in accordance with the Code of Virginia 15.2-2204. OR I move an alternative motion(s). The self-storage units/facility shall be developed and operated in substantial conformance with the concept plan and supporting materials submitted with the Special Use Permit application. 5. Any lighting that is provided on the property will be directed downwards, so as not to produce a glare onto adjacent properties or right-of-ways. 6. This condition is subject to modification in writing from VDOT prior to the operation. 8. All building code requirements required by the Uniform Statewide Building Code and/or the Page County Building Official shall be completed prior to the operation of the selfstorage units/facility. This condition is subject to modification in writing from the Page County Building Official prior to the operation. 9. All health requirements related to water and sewage required by the Virginia Department of Health shall be completed prior to the operation of the self-storage units/facility. This condition is subject to modification in writing from the Virginia Department of Health prior to the operation. 10. Any change of use or expansion of services not included in this special use permit will require an additional, new, or modified special use permit as required by the Page County Zoning Ordinance at that time. 11. The Zoning Administrator or their designated representative may visit the site at any time to ensure compliance with the special use permit. 12. Violations: This special use permit may be revoked upon material noncompliance with the terms of the permit, or upon violation of any other relevant terms of the Zoning Ordinance or any other ordinances of the County of Page, Virginia. However, prior to the commencement of any action to revoke this permit, the county shall notify the permit holder in writing of the material in noncompliance or violation, and the permit holder shall have thirty (30) days thereafter to cure the material non-compliance or violation. The notice shall be deemed given when hand delivered to the permit holder or when mailed by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the permit holder. I (we) the undersigned owner(s)/occupant(s) understand and agree to the foregoing conditions of this special use permit. I further understand that this special use permit may be reviewed on a yearly basis or at any time, the county determines necessary to ensure the compliance with and enforcement of all applicable conditions, codes, and regulations. ___ Owner(s) ___ Date ___ Board of Supervisors Chairman ___ Date ___ County Administrator ___ Date HARRISONBURG RESIDENCY LAND USE MEMORANDUM DATE: September 3, 2026 TO: Tracy Clatterbuck, CZA, Zoning Administrator I, Page County FROM: Burgess Lindsey, Area Land Use Engineer RE: Special Use Permit – Flowerdew Hundred LLC ___ VDOT has reviewed the following Special … (7) Small system wind energy facility. and WHEREAS, fire remains a serious public safety concern both locally and nationally, and the presence of lithium-ion batteries in many household devices introduces unique fire risks; and WHEREAS, most of the electronics used in homes daily — including smartphones, tablets, laptops, power tools, e-bikes, e-scooters, and toys — are powered by lithium-ion batteries, which if misused, damaged, or improperly charged, can overheat, start a fire, or explode; and WHEREAS, the National Fire Protection Association® (NFPA®) reports an increase in battery-related fires, underscoring the need for public education on the safe use of lithium-ion batteries and devices; and WHEREAS, the way lithium-ion battery devices are charged can make a difference in helping prevent home fires; and WHEREAS, safe charging includes using the cord and charger that came with your device or one approved by the manufacturer, charging on a hard, flat surface, watching for warning signs like devices that are very hot or start to swell, unplugging when fully charged, and charging larger devices like e-bikes outside and away from exits; and WHEREAS, residents are encouraged to understand that safe charging means making smart choices every time they plug in; and WHEREAS, Our Community’s first responders remain dedicated to reducing the occurrence of fires through prevention, safety education, and community outreach; and WHEREAS, the 2026 Fire Prevention Week™ theme, “Charge into Fire Safety™: Safe Charging Is a Superpower,” serves to remind all residents that safe charging can help reduce the risk of fires in homes and communities; THEREFORE, The Powhatan County Board of Supervisors do hereby proclaim October 4–10, 2026, as Fire Prevention Week and urge all residents to learn about and practice safe charging habits. and WHEREAS, domestic violence can take many forms, including physical, sexual, emotional, psychological, financial, and technological abuse, and is rooted in a pattern of power and control; and WHEREAS, one in three women and one in six men experience violence by an intimate partner during their lifetime, one in five homicide victims are killed by an intimate partner, and WHEREAS, victims and survivors in rural communities often face additional barriers to safety, including limited transportation, housing, shelter, and access to specialized services, making strong local resources and community partnerships especially important; and WHEREAS, every victim and survivor of domestic violence deserves to be heard, believed, and treated with dignity and compassion, without judgment, and to have access to the support, advocacy, resources, and choices needed to pursue safety, healing, stability, and independence; text: Board of Supervisors Agenda Summary Meeting Date: September 29, 2026 Item# : 2 Department: Solid Waste Staff Contact: Jeffrey L. Jones/Sarah Elam Puckett Agenda Item: Authorization to Proceed-Relocation/Underground of Landfill Power Line Summary: Attached for the Board's consideration is an invoice from Dominion Energy in the amount of $38,303.54 to relocate the main electrical service serving the County Landfill. Solid Waste General Manager, Jeff Jones has been working with LaBella and Dominion Energy since the spring to develop a plan to move the existing electrical infrastructure from the interior of the landfill to the northern perimeter. As the Board is aware, the next operational expansion of the landfill will be accomplished by "filling the valleys' of the current closed cells. This will include the area between Cells A,B,C,D and the 1997 cell and also between the 1997 and the pre-1988 cell. Relocating the electrical service now will: 1. Support construction of the new scalehouse and associated main entrance road improvements; and 2. Move the electrical infrastructure out of areas needed for current and future landfill operations and expansions. Noted on the attached map: X 0 Current poles from which power lines will be removed. The power poles will be left standin for coun staff to take down and re-use. Point from which power will begin to be run underground. New overhead power poles/line. Board approval tonight will allow Dominion to schedule the work and enable the electrical relocation to be coordinated with the construction of the new scalehouse/entrance improvements. No additional funding is required. Sufficient funding is available in the Landfill Construction Fund. ATTACHMENT: Dominion Construction Quote Landfill Map SAMPLE MOTION: I move that the Board authorize the Dominion Energy electrical relocation project and appropriate $38,303.54 from the Landfill Construction Fund. Call to Order, Pledge of Allegiance & Invocation: The pledge of allegiance will be led by Shawn Utt, County Administrator. The invocation will be provided by Stephanie Porter-Nichols. 2. Amendments to the Agenda: if any are necessary, they will be presented at the meeting. 3. Presentations a.
